speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROVISION OF MINIMUM PRICE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. The agricultural stabilization board has been authorized to provide a minimum price of $83 per ton for No. 1 peaches, 2-inch minimum size, delivered for processing in the province of Ontario. Under this authority the board will pay to the grower any amount by which the average return should fall below the prescribed price. The prescribed price of $83 per ton is about 89 per cent of the base or 10-year average price. This action has been taken to ensure that the peach growers will be able to market their crops. Inasmuch as the minister said last night that the estimates of his department were given very exhaustive and detailed study in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and that there was extensive questioning of witnesses, I do not think there is much point in my going over the same ground to any extent.
I just wish to say that I certainly appreciated being a member of the committee and being able to listen to the information given by the minister and the officials of his department. I want to publicly express my appreciation of the frank and open manner in which the discussions were held, and for the great amount of information and assistance given by the officials who were in attendance at the committee meetings.
The activities of this department probably have a far greater effect, from a material point of view, upon our society than those of any other department except the Department of Public Works. Those activities affect so many communities, industries and walks of life in our nation, and we in British Columbia are particularly dependent upon the attitudes and policies of the department. For instance our fishing industry, occupying such a great place in the economy of the province, is very much dependent upon the approach of the Department of Transport, especially as it relates to aids to navigation. I know the fishermen have expressed in years past, and will continue to do so in the years to come, their desire for additional aids to navigation and for the installation of more up to date and modern equipment for positioning, lighting and things of that nature.
In so far as aviation is concerned, the coast of British Columbia is a pretty difficult area in which to fly for a great portion of the year, and from that point of view also we are dependent to a great extent upon the approach of this department.
Shipping policies certainly affect my province, particularly the communities along

Supply-Transport
the coast line. Some of them are accessible by other means of transportation, but others are almost entirely dependent on shipping, and certainly the attitude of the government with respect to freight rates has a great effect upon our economy.
It is not my intention to go into detail as to the efficiency or otherwise of the department with respect to some of these questions, but I just wish to emphasize our dependence in British Columbia, as in the case of other provinces, on the attitude of this department. Probably there is only one respect of the department's operations which has no bearing on our affairs in British Columbia, and that is the aspect relating to canals. Try as we might, our efforts did not result in our being able to bring any need in this respect to the attention of the Minister of Transport. Apart from that, the activities of the department are watched with interest by workers and industrialists in British Columbia, and we hope that in future the approach will be even better than it has been in the past.
There is one problem I should like to mention briefly; and while this may be more specifically dealt with on the items relating to the Canadian maritime commission it might be just as well to mention it at this time. We might then be able to proceed with the rest of the estimates without too much difficulty or loss of time, inasmuch as the detailed and exhaustive analysis of the department was made in the standing committee.
Our merchant shipping fleet in Canada has been on the decline over the years, especially since the end of the last war. Ten or eleven years ago Canada was considered to have the fourth largest shipping fleet. Our fleet at that time numbered in the neighbourhood of 175 ships with a tonnage of 1,100,000. Then came a gradual decline in the number of ships under the Canadian flag, accompanied by a decline in tonnage and a decline in the amount of cargo carried by those ships, which would indicate that the policy of the government in this regard-and here we must look to the government which was in office during the period of this decline-was nothing more or less than one of allowing the merchant shipping fleet to wither on the vine and die an unnatural death, when it could very well have been expanded to include even more ships under the Canadian flag and employ even more Canadians in our own merchant fleet and handle our own commodities for export and import.
However, that has not been done, and we have seen this decline in shipping reach a point as at the end of March of last year where we had a total of 26 ships representing a gross tonnage of 186,165, only five ships being in the 10,000 ton class as far as cargo

ships are concerned. The balance was made up of smaller ships, diesel cargo ships, tankers, and so on. This decline in our Canadian merchant navy presents a sorry picture when it is considered that if the government of that day had taken an aggressive policy and abandoned its approach of holding in effect a fire sale of these ships after the last war, we might never have reached this position.
Unfortunately, I must say that I doubt very much whether the attitude of this present government is any better than that of its predecessor, because we have seen no great change in the policy of this government as compared with the government which was formerly in office. At what figure the number of merchant ships stands at the present time I do not know, but I imagine it is less than 26 ships, the figure given a year ago. Allowing the sale of the ships of the Canadian National fleet was not a good demonstration of this government's attitude with respect to attempting to build up our own merchant shipping fleet.
I have just these few remarks to make, and I will not go into more detail at this time. One could deal with these matters more extensively and better illustrate the deficiencies that have existed in past years with respect to this department, but I do not think it is necessary at this stage. Such questions can be dealt with more exhaustively in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines than in this committee.

Mr. Chairman, I wish this morning to discuss for a few moments a matter of special concern to my constituency and to a few others, that is the matter relating to shipyards.

(Text):
During the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I spoke about the very difficult situation facing the shipbuilding industry in Canada today, particularly in my constituency and others where many thousands of families depend on this industry for their livelihood. Earlier during the session the report of the royal commission on coastal trade was tabled in the House of Commons, and hon. members will now have had an opportunity of studying it. Those who have done this will notice that with respect to the most vital question of whether or not free competition with non-Canadian ships should be allowed in Canadian inland waters when the St. Lawrence seaway is completed the commission recommended in the affirmative, as the minister well knows. This recommendation, of course, was contrary to the request and arguments of the Canadian shipbuilding and repairing association and other organizations representing the shipbuilding industry. As a consequence Canadian shipbuilders today are very concerned, and I know the minister is well informed of this, about their future and the future of this important part of our national economy.
Of course I want to be fair about it and state that the problem of maintaining a prosperous shipbuilding industry in Canada did not arise overnight. At the beginning of the last war Canadian shipbuilders expanded their facilities very rapidly and were able to make a vital contribution to the allied war effort. However, since then the situation has become progressively worse for Canadian vessels. Construction costs are higher here than in the United Kingdom, and operating costs are also higher. So our shippers find it impossible to compete in international trade.
For this reason the last large group of 70 Canadian vessels was transferred to United Kingdom registry in 1949 and 1950. Transfers are still being made as new ships are built. Now that the Canadian National (West Indies) ships have been sold, the Canadian merchant fleet consists almost entirely of the vessels on the great lakes; and if with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway these boats too are to be faced with open competition from foreign vessels, then the minister will agree with me that the outlook for them is also very bleak.
It is for that reason that the Canadian shipbuilding and ship repairing association urged the following suggestions in its brief submitted to the royal commission on the coasting trade on June 30, 1955 as found at page 157 of the report of the commission:
1. That from henceforth the coasting trade of Canada shall be reserved to ships registered in Canada.
Supply-Transport
2. That from January 1. 1957, or some other convenient date in the near future, replacements of and additions to Canada's coasting fleet shall be built without exception in Canadian shipyards.
As I said at the beginning, the commission did not agree with this request. When the St. Laurent government set up the commission that was one of the most important questions it wished to have answered, but it was not the only question. If you read the order in council, P.C. 1955-308, appendix I of the report, setting up the commission you will find that Mr. Justice Spence and his colleagues were authorized and instructed to go much further than that. In fact they were authorized to study and recommend upon the whole subject of coastal shipping in Canada. So the present government is called upon to decide not only whether or not it will accept the royal commission's recommendation concerning open competition on our inland waters, but also the whole question of the future of our shipping industry.
When I spoke in the house on May 26 I mentioned some of the reasons why it is important to preserve our shipping industry in Canada. I referred to the serious consequences of closing down an industry employing some 15,000 people and supplying a livelihood to entire communities. I referred also to the importance of water transportation in the economic development of our country. As our economy grows our water transportation facilities must keep pace. If we are so convinced of the importance of water transportation as to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on the St. Lawrence seaway and other projects, surely we must be convinced as well of the importance of our merchant vessels to Canada's future. Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman, a nation with the most highly developed inland waterway in the world serving its ports and not having the necessary vessels to transport its own produce? It seems to me that our pride and confidence in Canada make it essential to find ways and means of maintaining our shipping industry, including the shipbuilding facilities which are the essential basis of a fleet.
There is also, Mr. Chairman, a third reason, and in my opinion a very important one, for maintaining our shipbuilding industry. We all remember in what an embarrassing situation Canada found itself when war broke out in 1939, when we had neither ships to come to the aid of Great Britain nor a navy suitable to protect such ships. The United Kingdom eventually managed to obtain 50 over-age destroyers from the United States for escort duty in exchange for military bases in Newfoundland and elsewhere. Our shipbuilders did heroic work, for which we have great cause to be grateful, in building ships to

Supply-Transport
transport men, munitions and supplies across
the Atlantic.
If we allow our shipyards to close down and disappear we risk finding ourselves in the same position as in 1939. After one severe lesson that is something which I think those responsible for the nation's security cannot ignore. Russia today has many more submarines than Hitler had in 1939. If war should be declared-and I am one who does not believe it would be over in a few hours-we would again be faced with the problem of keeping open the sea lanes between North America and our allies in Europe and other parts of the world. If the British shipping industry were to be destroyed, Canadian shipyards would then be the only ones in the commonwealth which could produce the ships necessary in wartime. So it is my contention that it is not only in Canada's interests but in the interests of the United Kingdom and all our allies that our shipbuilding industry be kept in readiness	as part of our military
preparedness.
Whatever the government decides to do, Mr. Chairman, about allowing foreign vessels to compete freely with Canadian vessels on the St. Lawrence waterway, it is of the utmost national importance for the government of Canada to take very positive steps to maintain our shipbuilding industry. Despite the fact that the Minister of Public Works has remained silent on this subject since becoming a minister of the crown, I still think I have his sympathy in this matter. If he and his colleagues would act now with the same force with which they used to criticize when they were in the opposition, then I think some way of helping the shipbuilding industry could be found. I was glad to notice that the royal commission on the coasting trade suggested that the shipbuilding industry might be assisted by a federal subsidy if seaway traffic from countries abroad worsens its positions.
I do not want to express negative criticism only on the question of shipbuilding. I want to place before the Minister of Transport a suggestion which I think merits some consideration, and which might serve to encourage the building of ships in Canada at this time. In one respect United Kingdom shippers, our keenest competitors, have what might be considered an unfair advantage over Canadian shippers. In addition to enjoying considerably lower construction and operating costs, they are able to claim 140 per cent of a vessel's value by way of tax deduction. In other words, a shipowner may claim as a deduction from his profit for tax purposes an investment allowance which when initiated in 1954 was 20 per
[Mr. Bourget.l
cent and now is 40 per cent of the cost of a ship. This is in addition to a normal depreciation allowance of 100 per cent over a period of years.
In the royal commission report, page 67, we find the following explanation given to the British House of Commons by the Chancellor of the Exchequer on April 9, 1957. He said this:
-the increase in the investment allowance is for ships only, and was proposed because of the special position of the shipping industry . . . faced with severe competition in a world market, often from ships sailing under flags of convenience with small liabilities. It finds it increasingly difficult to build up finance for the replacement of its ships when they become obsolete.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, if there is justification for the United Kingdom government helping its shipping industry in this way, a similar claim by Canadian shippers is justified. I am not suggesting that we should adopt a specific figure of 140 per cent in Canada, but perhaps the figure should be higher because the cost of building a ship in Canada, as the minister well knows, is approximately 60 per cent greater than the cost of building the same vessel in the United Kingdom.
For that reason I am not going to suggest a specific figure in this connection, but I do want to urge the Minister of Transport and the officials of the maritime commission to investigate this device and see whether, having regard to the fact that steel is no longer in short supply in Canada, the present would not be an appropriate time to introduce a measure of this kind, which seems to have given satisfaction abroad.
I do not forget, of course, that under the Liberal administration the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act was introduced, and it has been a very useful measure. I want to say, too, that it has been improved upon by the present minister, and at the time I complimented him and thanked him for doing so. I believe, having regard to the present economic situation, we need more than that. The minister quite realizes that this is an important industry and needs more help than we are giving it now.
The commission also recommended that the industrial development bank, which was set up by a Liberal government after the last war and which has done such a marvellous job in assisting the growth of smaller industries, should give serious study to providing adequate credit for the operators of small ships engaged in the coastal trade. The commission suggested that the future for ship repair work would be brighter as business picked up after the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway in 1959. However, with the average cost of building a ship in Canada

about 60 per cent higher than in Great Britain, there are tew possibilities of obtaining foreign, let alone Canadian, contracts in this country unless the government takes some action.
It seems to me that the object of government policy in this field should be to assure sufficient shipbuilding and repair work to enable our shipbuilding industry to survive and prosper to the greatest degree possible as our country develops. I view this as a matter of national importance. Let me read one paragraph from the commission report, which appears at page 178:
The commission is in no position to determine whether the defence preparedness value of a Canadian shipbuilding industry would be great enough to warrant it being maintained at a level of activity higher than is in prospect without assistance. Should this be determined to be the case, the commission considers that a policy of direct subsidization of ship construction would be the least costly and the most effective way of achieving the desired result.
This is a question for the government to decide, and on its decision the future of the shipbuilding industry depends. At the present time this is an industry worth more than $350 million and employing many thousands of Canadians. The Prime Minister indicated, when the report was tabled, that it would receive careful study. Well, Mr. Chairman, these thousands of Canadians are all looking to the federal government to help them in this critical situation. A solution must be found that will enable Canada to enjoy the benefit of economic ship transportation but which will, at the same time, enable our shipbuilding industry to survive.

Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity to ask the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to make a nation-wide survey of our railway requirements for the benefit of all districts which now have no railway service, so that they too might share in Canada's economic development.
Railroads and highways play a large part in the economic development of a country. They link areas together and ensure the economic future of an area. Highway and railway communications are like the blood vessels of the body. From the remotest corners of the land they bring in materials essential to large industrial production and farm products to non-farming areas.
In Canada's pioneer days, the waterways were the avenues of progress. That is why settlement was concentrated on both banks of the St. Lawrence, way up to the large inland sea, the great lakes. At that time there was no congestion, but due to the great distances, our forefathers had to fall back on a kind of economic self-sufficiency.
Supply-Transport
However, great modern discoveries gradually provided man with new and powerful means of venturing farther into the field of discovery and development. This opened up an era of artificial roads of communication entirely built by man according to his wants. Those linking roadways, railways, canals and highways marked, according to their purpose, the development of this vast country but favoured certain areas while keeping others back.
Thus some 40 per cent of the population of the province of Quebec is concentrated in the metropolitan area of Montreal.
The building of a coast-to-coast railroad was, to a great extent, the very lifeblood necessary for confederation to become a reality. It was a highly political decision, destined to promote progress inland as well.
There were other reasons why the province of Quebec was denied the railroads which would have meant greater industrial development for her. The former government, which held power for almost twenty-two years, neglected some areas and left them without needed railroads. This was typical of its neglect of the province of Quebec.
Thus, Quebec, with 30 per cent of Canada's population and a sprawling area, accounts for only 11 per cent of the railroad trackage, while regions with only a tenth of the population have equivalent trackage-or twice as much.
What is the sequel to this policy? Areas like Timiskaming, where, for twenty years, people have been clamouring for extension of the Montreal-Mont Laurier line, have, at best, remained static. The same applies to Gaspesia and other parts of Quebec-indeed, the entire country. Ore-rich areas like Chibougamau and Ungava, whose deposits were known practically half a century ago, are only at the dawn of their development, for people in the increasingly populous agricultural areas, unable to take part in the difficult development of industry in those parts where there are practically no communications, have been steadily forced to leave their village of origin, to take up residence in the big cities-even, alas, south of the border.
Mr. Chairman, allow me to draw your attention to a problem which exists in the town of Repentigny, in the federal riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I have repeatedly tried to get the Board of Transport Commissioners to follow up an urgent request by ordering the Bell Telephone Company of Canada to include that town in the "extended area service". Now, Repentigny is near the island of Montreal, to which it is linked by a bridge, "Le Gardeur de Repentigny". Almost all the towns around Montreal have now obtained the "extended area service"

from the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, and Repentigny, a fast growing community, urgently requires this service to keep up with the times; a number of new housing developments are under way and, all factors considered, no town in the whole of Canada is developing at a greater pace. His Worship Mayor Rosaire Deschamps and the aldermen of the town are clamouring for this "extended area service", realizing that the company's present service can only hamper present development and future prospects of this progressive town.
Mr. Chairman, quite apart from this lack of a basic service, Repentigny is putting up with an outrageous situation: 12-party lines -even 15-party lines! Fancy this-in the middle of the 20th century! It is enough to make Graham Bell turn over in his grave. It is unbearable for Repentigny residents. I grant that the Bell Telephone Company of Canada deserves a good deal of the credit for the country's economic progress, but it is high time it dipped into its kitty which still contains several million spare dollars, and put an end to this paralytic blow at Repentigny's development.
I call upon the Board of Transport Commissioners to instruct the Bell Telephone Company of Canada to resolve this pressing problem as soon as possible, to the satisfaction of those concerned.
Mr. Chairman, may I, in conclusion, congratulate the Minister of Transport for the admirable way in which he performs his duties, and for his bilingualism-symbol of national unity.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to several matters that are extremely important to the riding I represent, and I think in a general way they are important to many other parts of Canada. In Lincoln county we are particularly interested in shipbuilding, water transportation and air transportation. First of all I should like to express my opposition to tolls on the Welland ship canal. Since the canal cuts across the Niagara peninsula I am well aware of the type of ships that use the canal and the type of cargoes that pass through it.
Briefly I should like to say something about the several canals that have been built in the Niagara peninsula during the last 130 years. Three canals in all have been built. I shall deal with the first one and also with the third canal, which is the one in use at the present time. The first canal was built by private enterprise with some financial assistance from the government of Upper Canada and the British government in London at that time. As it was a canal that was built by private

enterprise, tolls were charged. In 1841 the capital stock of this canal company was acquired by the government of Canada, and since that time Welland ship canals have been entirely under the control and maintenance of the government of Canada and thus toll free.
About 70 years ago the first canal was discontinued as a ship canal, and since that time it has gradually deteriorated into a public nuisance, dangerous to health and public safety. Without going into full details in connection with the clean-up of this canal, I must say that negotiations with the Department of Transport have been going on since 1934. However, it fell to our present Minister of Transport to conclude the negotiations with the area municipalities. Preliminary work is now started, and the balance of the contracts will be let for the clean-up before the end of the year.
To turn to the present Welland canal, as I say tolls were discontinued many years ago, just as tolls were discontinued on our public highways, all in the interests of a freer development of Canada. A toll free Welland canal is a custom of long standing, and has been a matter of settled international policy for many years. To change that policy now could bring about retaliation by the United States of America, and tolls could be placed on the upper lakes channels that have been improved and maintained by the United States and have also been toll free. Industry and commerce throughout the entire upper great lakes region, in which there are large industrial areas both in the United States and Canada, have relied upon the established policies of no tolls. The imposition of tolls now would tend to destroy this stability and could discourage new industries from locating in these areas. Even a small toll on the Welland ship canal such as that recommended by the joint tolls committee establishes a new policy, and implies that further tolls may be imposed when further improvements and enlargements are made to the canal.
I believe that this is the time to make a decision against the levying of tolls on the Welland canal and to clarify its future operational authority. Industry located on the Welland canal and those considering locating in that area should know the future policy of the Canadian government with respect to this matter.
The Welland ship canal is different from other parts of the seaway and other parts of the great lakes navigation system. It is entirely owned by the government of Canada and lies well within the boundaries of Canada.
I believe that this canal, located as it is,

should remain entirely owned by the government of Canada and operated by the Department of Transport, and should be toll free. There seems to be no need to have it under international seaway authority.
When I say the Welland ship canal is toll free and should continue that way, it does not mean that ships pass through the locks entirely free of charge. At the present time ships using the canal pay a locking charge to cover the cost of linesmen, supplied by the Department of Transport, who assist in tying up the boats when they pass through the locks. Industries located along the canal pay substantial charges for use of water, wharfage and other rentals, all of which is applied against the operational costs. This revenue from locking charges, rentals, use of water and wharfage amounts to something over $1 million annually, and the annual cost of operation and maintenance amounts to slightly over $2 million.
A review of these annual revenues should be made. I am informed that no increases have been made since 1932. Upward revisions, perhaps, could be made to bring revenues more in line with operating costs. The basic charge for locking a vessel through the canal is $25 for smaller vessels up to 250 feet long, and $50 for the larger ones. I believe it takes from four to eight linesmen on each lock to make the ships fast. There are eight locks, and it takes about eight to ten hours for a ship to pass through the entire length of the canal. I think there is reason to review this matter in order to bring our costs more in line.
Much of the cargo passing through the canal consists of Canada's natural resources including wheat, oil, pulpwood and iron ore. Tolls will only increase the cost of our wheat in Liverpool and our pulpwood, iron ore and oil in central Canada and the United States. We in the Niagara peninsula look forward with confidence in the expectation that with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway it will be possible for coal from Nova Scotia and iron ore from the north shore of Quebec to compete with coal and iron ore from the United States. A toll free Welland ship canal would do much to make that possible.
I was interested to note in yesterday's press that Nova Scotia coal is now being delivered in the Toronto area. I believe this is the first time this has happened in a good many years, perhaps the first time it has ever happened. This is something we must encourage, but making it more expensive to sail on our waterways by the imposition of tolls is not going to help the situation. Tolls on the Welland ship canal and the upper
Sup p ly-Transport
lake channels might very well destroy some of the advantages which could be ours when the seaway is complete and larger vessels can be used. At such a time more direct shipments could be made of our raw material and natural resources. I trust that if the final decision on tolls is made by the cabinet when parliament is not in session, all the facts and forecast outlined in the many briefs which have been presented to the seaway authority and to the Department of Transport regarding the Welland ship canal will be thoroughly considered.
I would also like to mention the use of pilots on the great lakes by deep sea vessels. There seems to be a strong opinion in certain quarters that pilots are not necessary on the open lake but only when those ships are passing through the St. Lawrence seaway itself or the Welland ship canal, or are entering harbours and restricted channels. I understand, however, that our navigational signs and signals are quite different from those used under deep sea regulations. There is also, in many cases, a language problem in connection with foreign ships. For these reasons, and as a matter of safety for other vessels, I should think the captains of these deep sea vessels should have to undergo some test or examination before they are allowed to sail on any part of the great lakes system.
Another matter which I would bring to the attention of the minister is that of the pollution of our lake shore beaches by the discharge of sewage and industrial waste into our lakes, canals and water courses by the cities and towns. Many of our beaches on lake Ontario and lake Erie are becoming unsafe for bathing as a result of pollution from oil scum carelessly discharged from ships, untreated sewage and industrial waste. This is a matter which requires immediate attention, and it is one which is of more concern to the Department of National Health and Welfare. Nevertheless in the past the Department of Transport has given to municipalities and industries leases which permit the discharge of sewage and industrial waste into canals and water courses under the jurisdiction of the department.
I hope the minister will give this matter serious consideration. I know it is going to cost a lot of money to the city of St. Catharines; nevertheless it is something which must be faced, and the sooner we do it the better.
I would suggest to the Department of Transport that it should continue its interest in establishing regional airports in strategic areas, in providing services for feeder air lines, in picking up scheduled air services and

Supply-Transport
by providing intermediate service to relieve the larger air terminals which are now badly congested.
Another matter which I am sure concerns all of us is the passing of our coastal and ocean going ships into the hands of foreign operators. In particular, the passing of Canadian steamships into Cuban registry has not constituted a solution to our problem. I am familiar with a small Canadian company which is being forced into the same position which, by the way, is a St. Catharines firm. I refer to the Ahearn Steamship Company, which over the past five or six years has been engaged in hauling supplies into the Northwest Territories. Ships of European registry are now cutting into that trade and paying about one-third of the wages. And having a much lower standard of living for their sailors, they are taking away the business from our Canadian companies, and as a consequence this company I have mentioned now has only one of its four boats in operation.
I have in my hand a clipping from a labour magazine in which I was interested, having been associated with labour organizations at one time, and unless they have changed their ways their reports are generally pretty accurate. This particular report says that the Canadian government has sent a fleet of 52 ships into the Arctic carrying freight and military supplies, and of those 52 vessels only two bear Canadian registry. One of these is a ship of the Ahearn Steamship Company I believe and the other the Maple-branch, is from somewhere down in Nova Scotia. I think this is a very serious matter, requiring the consideration of the government. If nothing is done about it, then it will not be long before ships of Canadian registry will no longer be operating on the great lakes. Their trade is already being cut into to a great extent.
Mr. Chairman, my remarks have probably been rather rambling, but I appreciate the opportunity of bringing to your attention and that of the minister the problems of the county I represent. I am sure the minister will give them this serious consideration, as he did in connection with the clean-up of the old canal.

Mr. Chairman, Dominion day this year, the 91st anniversary of Canada's confederation, marked the completion of the major works in the building of the St. Lawrence seaway and power project. It was the day on which the rushing waters of the St. Lawrence poured into a basin above the international St. Lawrence power dam. It

was the day on which a new lake was born. According to the statement by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys made in the house on August 20, the lake has now been named lake St. Lawrence. The minister said that was the choice of the Canadian board on geographical names. I have no quarrel with this particular board, but it seems to me that the name is meaningless.
I thought here was an occasion to name this lake after a Canadian who had rendered outstanding service in the promotion of the St. Lawrence project. On August 4 last I asked the Minister of Transport the following question:
Is the goverment contemplating naming the newly created lake in the St. Lawrence seaway in the near future? If so, is the suggestion contained in the letter to the editor to be considered?
A letter to the editor of the Ottawa Citizen which appeared in the issue of Saturday, August 2, impressed me with the idea that here perhaps was a suggestion which, regardless of political affiliation, was good and had real merit. I wish now to quote the letter which I was prevented from reading because, apparently, I was out of order in attempting to do so at that time:
I understand our authorities are looking for a suitable name for the new lake in the St. Lawrence. I believe a Canadian name would be well received especially the name of one who had so much to do with the getting together of the United States and Canada in the formation and completion of this great project. I know most Canadians and Americans appreciate the efforts of Mr. Seaway himself, Mr. Lionel Chevrier, M.P. What man in Canada whether Conservative or Liberal is more entitled to a thank you for a job he did. than Mr. Chevrier?
I believe lake Chevrier would be well received by the Canadian public in general and would also show that the present government appreciates the work of this great Canadian for services rendered whether Conservative or Liberal.
I do not know whether the minister is very happy about the choice, or whether he or the government ever gave any consideration to naming the lake, but it seems to me that the government should have seized the occasion to honour a person, preferably one who has had more to do with the actual planning of the great project than any other Canadian, by virtue of the position he held in the Canadian government of the day and subsequently as chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway commission.
I would say that the name "Chevrier" would have met with the approval of a large majority of Canadians. The large French Canadian population living along the shores of the seaway would have appreciated one of their favourite sons being so honoured.
Will the minister take all these factors into consideration and perhaps recognize the former minister of transport in some manner,

so that the name "Chevrier" will be associated with what has been undoubtedly one of the most talked about projects in the world, ranking alongside the building of the Suez and Panama canals?
Along the great lakes 8,300 miles of shore line, cities in the great mid-west of the United States will become ocean ports. The city of Chicago will be linked with Calcutta, Duluth, Antwerp, Toronto, Brisbane, Australia; General Motors of Canada will be able to ship a Chevrolet or a Cadillac to New Zealand for less money than it now costs to ship a car from Oshawa to Vancouver by rail; wheat will move from Fort William, Ontario to Rotterdam at a saving of up to 15 cents per bushel.
This is a reality of the near future, and what could be more exciting than to have Her Gracious Majesty Queen Elizabeth sailing along this great seaway on the royal yacht Britannia from Montreal to Fort William on the official opening of this magnificent project? A suggestion along these lines has already been communicated to the Prime Minister, and I understand that his office and Buckingham Palace are considering the idea.
The broad outline of the Queen's third visit to Canada next year would indicate that a voyage starting at Montreal and ending at Fort William would give Her Majesty and her sailor-minded husband one of the greatest possible opportunities for sheer enjoyment and relaxation, and would permit brief stops at major points on both sides of the international boundary.
I express the hope that the Minister of Transport and the government will do everything in their power to plan the official opening of this great project, in which the Queen will participate, in such a manner that it will go down in history as the most memorable Canadian event of the century.
There is another matter I should like to mention, and that is the effective role which Trans-Canada Air Lines is playing in the transportation field in our nation. This is at least one of the beneficial projects which the former Liberal government created, the chief architect of which was the former brilliant minister of trade and commerce, Right Hon. C. D. Howe. Trans-Canada Air Lines has an enviable record of efficiency and I wish to congratulate the president, Mr. G. R. McGregor, and his capable staff for the very courteous handling of passengers.
Now I would like to ask the minister if he is giving consideration to granting transportation privileges on T.C.A. to members of parliament on the same basis that is now enjoyed in connection with the railways.
Supply-Transport
There are a goodly number of us who cannot possibly use the railways due to the time factor. Surely any member whose riding is 500 miles or more from Ottawa should have the privilege and the convenience of visiting his constituency as often as possible without being compelled to be away too long from his parliamentary duties.
I understand the minister was wholeheartedly in favour of the free use of the services of T.C.A. for members when he sat on this side of the house. May I ask him if he is still in favour of the idea-I hope he is- and may I also express the hope that he will see his way clear to make a statement on the matter which will give us all hope that we may expect the implementation of what he himself has advocated in the past, if not during the present session, which is nearing its end, then in forthcoming sessions of this parliament.

Mr. Chairman, because the minister's estimates have been very thoroughly examined by the standing committee and because of their lateness in coming before us this session I am going to be most parsimonious in dipping into the barrel of time on this occasion. However, I should be remiss if I did not bring to the attention of the minister one or two matters which are still of very serious concern to my constituents.
Before doing that, however, I do want to say that after reading the minutes of the committee on estimates and Mr. Gordon's evidence I, like a good number of other Canadians who read reports of the same evidence in the newspapers, am very disturbed at the suggestion by Mr. Gordon that there is a need for the curtailment of the transcontinental passenger service in this country. I am one of a good many who hope this will not be necessary, and I think that in this respect the C.N.R. is somewhat at fault for a certain lack of patronage. I am not sure that everyone will agree with me, but I believe that with respect to transcontinental passenger trains The Canadian, which operates under the C.P.R., is probably the best train today; and hon. members can imagine how it pains me to admit that at this time.
These railways are the fundamental basis of our transportation system. Regardless of the possibilities of air travel and travel by road, we must realize that at all times during the year our heavy freight and commodities must go by railroad, and that in bad weather the great majority of people want to go by railroad, too. It is essential that we maintain our railroad system in Canada and our first class passenger service.

Supply-Transport
I realize the difficulties; the demand for air travel, for water travel, for improved transportation by highways and the carrying of freight by trucks, and so on. We are inclined to want everything at once without regard to the circumstances. I believe the whole situation in Canada with respect to transportation of all types shows a lack of planning, and illustrates the need for consideration of the entire problem from a national point of view and the development of a national transportation policy.
I have noticed from conversations with employees and with somewhat senior officials of the Canadian National Railways that there is a lowering of the morale of the staff of that company across Canada at this time. I am not blaming the management entirely for that. It is occasioned to some extent by large lay-offs in certain places involving men 45 years of age and over, who have given the very best years of their lives to the railway and who have an investment in their homes in the communities in which they have lived for many years. I have also noticed a certain lowering of morale amongst the supervisory staff, occasioned by the fact that there is a somewhat different approach to railroading nowadays from the approach that obtained in the old days.
Going back approximately 50 years I remember that some of the older officials of the C.P.R., the men who operated the railroad, were railroaders from the ground up. The railroads are now managed by business administrators and executives, to a large extent, and in my opinion and in the opinion of many people they have not the same human approach to problems as they affect the employees and the communities which the railways were designed to serve.
I have personal knowledge of many cases of men who have served the company well for a long period of years. I believe these remarks apply to both the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. These men have long experience and have given many years of good service. They find themselves denied promotion today because someone who has just graduated from a university with a degree in engineering or a bachelor of arts degree is considered more suitable for positions in these circumstances. I would not want to underestimate the value of those degrees and academic qualifications generally, but I feel that both the railways could give more serious con-
sideration when they are making promotions in the middle supervisory class to those men who have experience and who have served the railways over a number of years.
In addition, it was recently brought to my attention that the C.N.R. has made an agreement with the Pacific Great Eastern Railway to haul its empty box cars from the coast to the interior for 5 cents a mile per box car. I do not know what the details of the arrangements are, but the information I obtained from people closely in touch with the administration of the C.N.R. in that division is that it will have the effect of taking traffic away from the C.N.R. without providing any substantial saving. I mention those facts because these older employees of both railways have no one to speak for them with respect to their complaints in general as they apply to the parliament of Canada, except members of parliament.
I now come to a more local problem, and I can tell from the look of anticipation on the part of the minister that he is eagerly looking forward to hearing what I have to say.
Always.

In our own district we
believe that the C.P.R. has been most unthoughtful in its consideration of the needs of the people of the district so far as passenger service is concerned, and has completely overlooked the great contribution that the Kootenays make to the industrial production of Canada. They have done that by reducing service in two ways. First of all, they have reduced the number of days the trains operate on the Kettle Valley railroad between Vancouver and Nelson; and second, they have reduced the service by running a Budd car without any sleeping accommodation or any cafe car for the serving of meals.
This has been brought to the minister's attention very forcefully by representatives of various organizations in my constituency which he visited during the election period last year in an effort to try and make certain that I did not return to this house. I do not blame him for that; that was his duty, and we all have to accept our responsibilities in that respect. However, it has been brought to his attention and it is continually being brought to his attention, as it is to mine. I represent a type of people who never cease agitating until they reach their objective.

They have the same attitude with respect to peacetime affairs as the 54th battalion had overseas in the war.
With respect to the reduction of service I wish to read a letter that was written by the local chairman of the brotherhood of railroad trainmen, Kootenay lodge No. 558, Nelson, British Columbia on July 31. The letter is addressed to Mr. G. L. Phillips, superintendent, C.P.R., at Nelson, British Columbia, and a copy was sent to me. The letter states the position from the point of view of the men who are operating the trains: Dear Sir:
I have been instructed by the members of the brotherhood of railroad trainmen and other running trades to vigorously protest to you, the company attitude and manner in regards to the curtailment of service on the boundary subdivision.
On Sunday July 27. passenger train No. 45. two diesel units and four passenger cars was run from Nelson to Midway on the boundary subdivision, leaving Nelson at 9.00 a.m., arriving Midway at
1.20	p.m. A freight train extra 4064 east was run out of Midway on the same date, leaving Midway at
1.20	p.m. arriving at Nelson at 10.00 p.m. with ten loads and two empties.
The fact that the two above mentioned trains have been run on a day and weekend at which time a curtailment of service is supposed to be in effect is sufficient to prove that other trains could be run seven days a week under the same conditions.
The people in our district, the people in general as well as employees of the railway, are of the opinion that the C.P.R. is taking advantage of the particular circumstances in the Kootenay district, where on occasions the railway track has been blown up, to reduce the passenger service. In their opinion the very fact that freight trains can operate continuously is an indication that the company is taking advantage of this situation to reduce that service.
With respect to the Budd car, we find this is a most unpleasant means of travel. It is particularly difficult for older people coming from the coast because it involves a 22-hour trip in a Budd car with no sleeping accommodation provided and no opportunity to obtain meals in a proper manner. A newsboy does come around periodically with a pot of coffee and dried up sandwiches, but that is not suitable nutrition for elderly people, children and those who are sick.
I have outlined my complaints on behalf of the people I have the honour to represent, and I urge the minister to do all he can to ease the situation by discussing the matter again with the board of transport commissioners and the officials of the C.P.R. to see if something cannot be done to meet the very modest requests of my constituents.

Mr. Chairman, I believe it was just a week ago today that I rose to make some comments on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare,
Supply-Transport
on which occasion you offended my sensibilities and caused me deep grief by suggesting that I was making a political speech. I was grievously hurt at your suggestion, because that was the farthest thing from my mind and because you know I never indulge in activities of that kind. I thought it was a general, rough and tumble discussion in which anyone could join, and I felt moved to participate in the discussion on that occasion.
However, a different situation obtains today. I am rising to speak on the estimates of the Department of Transport, and I want to join the happy throng who have jumped on the bandwagon and become one of the members of the mutual admiration club that has been operating since the minister concluded his remarks. In doing so I wish to extend him my compliments and congratulate him on the efficient administration of his department.
It was a revelation to me to find, shortly after I became a member of the house, that no matter from what constituency a member came or to what party he belonged, all of them, whether they were ordinarily extreme free traders or high protectionists, had one thing in common when it was a question of their own riding, municipality or province. They were all outstanding high protectionists. They wanted everything they could possibly get to protect their own ridings.
But today we have a general give-away, with each one after a bridge or a canal or a post office or an airport, and the Minister of Transport is acceding to their requests. I was particularly pleased last night when the hon. member for Laurier presented his request. He outlined his connection with the department over a period of years and complimented the minister upon carrying out some of the policies he had inaugurated and adding a few others that pleased him as well. He spoke about the St. Lawrence seaway, referred to the Lachine section, requested that the Quebec hydro authorities be given consideration with respect to development and mentioned an amount in the neighbourhood of $6 million which, with today's inflation, would represent a sum of approximately $20 million.
I was exceedingly pleased at the alacrity with which the minister acceded to the request of the hon. member, and the fact that the minister said he would go as far as he possibly could. It brings to mind what a difference a few years make, because I can remember the continual trek to Ottawa over the years by Sir Adam Beck when he was just plain Adam Beck, the father of hydro development in the province of Ontario. I can

Supply-Transport
remember how all during his regime, and subsequently Mr. McGrath, Mr. Cook, Mr. Lyon and Bob Saunders, all of whom had the interests of Ontario hydro and the province at heart, he came down here year after year to plead for development of the power potential on the St. Lawrence only to meet with obstacles, stumbling blocks and frustrations and have to go back home after fruitless journeys. The St. Lawrence seaway was known at that time as the deep sea waterway, later as the great lakes waterway and finally the St. Lawrence seaway.
No matter what party was in power the same answer was always given. No recognition was given to their pleas. In addition to having tremendous energy, Sir Adam Beck possessed marvellous powers of foresight in being able to peer into the future and assess the requirements of the province of Ontario and the whole dominion. He had an analysis made of the power potential of the province. He outlined what was going to be required. He pointed out that when Niagara power was exhausted Ontario hydro would probably have to call upon the province of Quebec to assist them, because Ontario hydro was then supplying eastern Ontario by bringing power from Niagara Falls.
The hon. member for Laurier mentioned the wonderful hydro development that has taken place in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway and said that he thought that Premier Frost should consider allotting some of the power from the St. Lawrence seaway development to the eastern section of Ontario in the same way as is being done by the New York state power authority across the river. I can assure the hon. member that Ontario hydro has always endeavoured to take care of the eastern part of the province, even going to the extent of bringing in power from Niagara Falls and elsewhere.
But the situation is different today. We have this power development now on the St. Lawrence seaway after 25 or 30 years of making appeals and being blocked by the electrical ring and commercial interests, some of the opposition emanating from the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal. The same thing happened in the case of Sir Adam Beck. The power ring in the United States concentrated all their efforts to frustrate everything Sir Adam Beck did in the interests of the people of Canada, particularly the people of the province of Ontario. If I were to follow the technique of the opposition groups of saying that we do not start things soon enough and do not go far enough I could point out that the St. Lawrence seaway is an outstanding example of that, in that it was not started soon enough and did not go far enough under the previous administration.

However, we are indulging in happy, mutual approbation today and complimenting each other upon the wonderful results of the St. Lawrence seaway. Nevertheless there is one thing I regret. I do not want to be too severe because of the nice-Nellie diplomatic policy of the previous administration in dealing with the United States, but things came to the point where we were so fed up with the opposition to the seaway project that we finally told the United States that if they were not going to participate in the project we would go ahead and build it and pay for it ourselves.
I thank the hon. member for Laurier for expressing appreciation of the services of Bob Saunders in abating the opposition in the United States and getting them to cooperate with the province of Ontario with respect to power. Be that as it may, the United States came to the conclusion that we were going to be tough about it and would go ahead. Therefore though they were reluctant to do so, they agreed to take part in the project. But after that our tough policy was watered down. It became lukewarm and the United States eventually took over and dictated the whole policy as far as the St. Lawrence seaway was concerned.
I will not say anything more about the building of the St. Lawrence seaway and the fact that we did not go far enough because we did not build our own canal system within the Dominion of Canada. I will leave that to another time later, because I do not want to mar the love and sweetness evident in this debate, and also because I know the minister would like to get these estimates through.
To change the subject for a moment, I am pleased that the amount of money available under the grade crossing fund has been increased. In that regard may I say to the hon. member for Laurier that I appreciated his attitude when he was the minister of this department and the matter of the grade crossing fund came up. I had always been vitally interested in it, and I still am. At that time I put forward a plea for further consideration by the government, but I was ruled out of order because the matter was under quasijudicial consideration by the board of transport commissioners. However, I was very much concerned because in my riding there were some 11 level crossings where serious accidents had happened, and likewise in the adjoining riding of Scarborough there were 82 level crossings, 52 of which were considered hazardous because of accidents. I was, therefore, bringing the matter before the house knowing that I was out of order, but the hon. member for Laurier allowed me to practically complete my remarks before he

raised his objection. I want to say that I appreciated that very much.
When the report did come in it was worth waiting for, and I feel that the minister did his best at that time to increase the amount of money that is available. However, there was not sufficient consideration given to the matter because, in fact, there are very few votes in that proposition. At any rate, I think they are on the right track, and they are going to speed up the progress of removing this menace from the Dominion of Canada.
The other matter I should like to mention is one to which the hon. member for Kootenay West referred. The last time I was talking about it the hon. member was introducing a bill. While he was out of order, I joined with him in placing before the house some of the claims I thought should be made in regard to the railways. I have not changed my opinion on that. He has referred to the attitude of the president of the Canadian National Railways, and I think serious consideration should be given to that matter. I do not say it is an amusing thing, though sometimes it is, but it is alarming when the president of a great concern can come to our committee and, with the nonchalance of a person who is enjoying himself, tell the committee that we are going to have a deficit next year; that the railway is going to have to remove this particular service or reduce it. He did not have to tell us he was reducing the service, because everyone is aware of it. He says he is not getting the passengers, but he is not giving the service that the people of Canada require of him, and if it keeps on he will not have anyone riding on his passenger cars.
I pointed out to hon. members at that time the situation with regard to the stations at Ottawa and Toronto, as well as other places. I referred to the lack of service and the complete contempt in which the people travelling on the railroad are held. I thought there might be some prospect of a change in that situation, but no change whatever has taken place. I think it was a Mr. Dunn who was in charge of the service here who admitted that everything I said was correct but there was not much that they could do about it. It was one of those things with which we had to put up. They were going to move the station some five miles away soon, and the long-suffering public would have to put up with that until then.
There is the attitude of a railway that is operating on a deficit, for which you and I and all the people of Canada have to dig down into our pockets to pay. They cannot improve the service with these half-baked policies, these half-considered plans which are in effect today. Probably it would be a good idea if we called them in and said,
Supply-Transport
"We are going to cut your salary in half because of the service you are giving." Probably we could say to Mr. Gordon, "All right; you are taking it so nonchalantly, how would you like your salary cut from $75,000 to $37,500?" If a private business were operated like that, there would either be a new manager very soon or the business would close down.
I have a clipping from a newspaper here which says that they are going to discontinue operating the passenger service to Owen Sound and Wiarton. There is probably some reason for curtailing that service, but they are going to continue the freight trains, and there would be no more expense involved in having a passenger car on the freight train. They said they would discontinue that service because they were not getting any passengers. Well I claim there will be no harm in leaving the passenger coach on the freight train that is to be continued; it will cost very little. The clipping goes on:
The company further applied for licences which would enable it to carry by road transport the mail, express and passenger baggage formerly carried by two Montreal-Brockville trains.
The railway said it proposes to serve all railway stations and express agencies on the line between Montreal and Brockville with trucks which would operate on highway No. 2 and others, and county roads.
That is a capital idea. At last they have a certain amount of wisdom and they are going to give faster service by using trucks. It is because of the slowness of the passenger service the railways were giving that people are using automobiles. I wish they would apply this to the railway section between Brockville and Ottawa. I wish they would take off those super-duper freight cars that they call express cars and baggage cars, and for which they have all kinds of freight and postal equipment. These cars form such a large part of the train that when you come to the station you have to crawl over crates and large trucks used for hauling away this freight and express.
Since the last time I mentioned this the railways have added another inconvenience. They just dump the ice on the platform in large blocks before putting it in the cooling system of these cars. You have to jump over that, and probably if you miss the jump and light on the slab of ice, you slide into the station on your backside. Just imagine my chagrin last Thursday when I was returning from the opening of the exhibition in Toronto. The Minister of Transport had to suffer the indignity of having to walk through the passenger cars up to the baggage cars before getting out in order to try to avoid walking through the rain. There were so many of these baggage cars on the train that the

Supply-Transport
passenger cars were down to the Laurier avenue bridge and the passengers had to walk through the rain right into the station. I said to the Minister of Transport, "Can you imagine that happening to us?"
Shame.

Imagine that kind of service, when the Minister of Transport has to walk through all this rain and lose the press in his trousers to get to the station. I said, to our dapper Minister of Transport, "George, I think the next time we will have to get you the Governor General's car so you can be brought right into the station." Then, if they do not give better service, we shall have to carry this thing further. I think we would accomplish marvellous results if we were to bring in Mr. Gordon and say, "You are a swell fellow, and you can tell us how much you deficit is going to be, how much it is going to cost with your broken-down equipment, but we think your salary should be commensurate with the service."
He tells us that the parlour cars, the sleeping cars and so on are going concerns, that they produce a profit. At the same time they treat travellers with the utmost contempt. Hon. members have great difficulty in securing accommodation if they want to leave here on a Friday or Saturday night. They are told there is a waiting list, so you must wait for cancellations to get accommodation. When we receive that kind of treatment from a service that is producing a profit I think it is time we broughi in Mr. Gordon and talked to him in a lovey-dovey fashion, saying, "We do not want to hurt your feelings, but we think the time has arrived when your salary should be commensurate with the kind of service you are giving, and probably at $25,000 a year you would be overpaid."

We were, of course, greatly interested in what was said by the hon. member who just took his seat, especially in the opening portion of his remarks when he joined hands in a very affectionate way with the opposition and congratulated the former minister of transport for the attitude he takes toward the present minister. But somehow or other I think the hon. member perhaps resorted to the type of caution that he always exercises in the statements he makes. He has always been very careful in every way he expresses himself to retain unity in the country, to retain unity as between the parties. With that same type of caution which he previously exhibited in this house, he now proceeds to reverse himself. I do not know why at this juncture he becomes critical in a way which, judging from his remarks, led me to believe that

maybe the hon. member for Danforth is looking for an appointment or seeking a job in the railway service of Canada.
Oh, heaven help me, no.

I do not know that, but that is the impression I received. After all, I think the hon. member has referred to a very fine civil servant of this country who, over the years and in difficult days in time of war, has been exemplary in giving the kind of service that Canadians should give to their country. There may be some criticism which might be made of the railway operation or of the railway system, but I do not think it is within the right of members of the House of Commons to speak in a fashion that is not appropriate with regard to a distinguished citizen of Canada and a prominent civil servant.
There was the suggestion, for example, that the minister himself had perhaps experienced some inconvenience in having to walk a little distance in the rain. This was typical of the humility which the minister has always shown in his new office. There is no hauteur about him. He is humble in his ways. He lives with the people. That is one of the things which I am sure prompted the hon. member for Laurier to congratulate him so fully and sincerely on his appointment.
I want to join in that congratulation. We find the Minister of Transport to be a most congenial gentleman. He is affable. Above all, Mr. Chairman, he is easily approachable; he receives you like a colleague in the house. He is really a splendid gentleman. With all these qualities, being a humble man and one who does not mind if he is obliged to walk several yards in the rain, the minister should be congratulated. Certainly he should be the first one to complain if he was not pleased with the situation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He might even sing "Walking in the Rain".

As I said, he does not look any the worse for his experience. I am sure he has not suffered by it. However, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something that is not intended to be critical.
The minister disturbed much of the thinking around the city of Montreal when he announced recently that there will be no air conditioning for the Dorval airport. That announcement was a disturbing one. The minister may have given good reasons, but it is my objective at this time, if I can, to persuade the minister to reconsider whether or not the new Dorval airport merits air conditioning. I should like to point out that there is a substantial increase in air travel, and that there will be a further increase in

the future. Montreal is the showplace of Canada to incoming air passengers, whether from the United States or from Europe. Montreal airport will make the first impression upon visitors or newcomers to our country. Having gone to the tremendous expense of erecting such a magnificent building, I think it is a little shortsighted not to complete it to the fullest extent. Certainly in a few more years air conditioning will be prevalent everywhere, in every public building. Why then wait a few more years and be obliged to tear down sections and instal air conditioning? The time to instal it is now. It will be done at a great saving if it is done now.
I should also like to point out not only that Montreal is the showplace to incoming passengers but that we must also consider first impressions. People coming to Canada and being received at such a magnificent airport certainly are being dealt with by civil servants. The immigration branch, for example, should have the comfort and the convenience of air conditioning when they are examining passengers, when passengers are sitting before them, are being questioned and cross-questioned and are having to spend time there. Imagining how uncomfortable the situation could be on a hot July day for incoming passengers on their first trip to Canada, being in this gorgeous building and sitting and sweltering in the heat before an immigration official. Apart from the fact that answering questions is a trying experience-being alert to answer properly-there is that added discomfort.
Then, of course, you also have the customs branch. Why should not the customs officials enjoy the convenience of air conditioning? Everywhere in public buildings it is possible to enjoy it. The customs officials must exert themselves physically in the lifting up of baggage, in the lowering of baggage, in opening it and in closing it, and in examining the baggage of passengers. On a hot sweltering day it is not a very comfortable occupation. I am sure the hon. member for Danforth would not like it. Does the minister wish to say something?

If I may, Mr. Chairman; I see that it is about one o'clock. I should like to thank the hon. member for his very constructive remarks, and also to assure him and other hon. members from the Montreal area that since I made my announcement in the house, my officials and I have been doing a great deal of thinking about this matter with a view to seeing whether something can be done. I am very hopeful that something can be done, and that it will be possible to make a statement to that effect in the very near future. I thank the hon. member
Supply-Transport
for what he has said, and I agree with him. Everything possible is being done to work out something along those lines and, as I have said, I hope to be able to make in the very near future the kind of statement that he would like me to make.

With that assurance, Mr. Chairman, I have nothing further to add, and I shall conclude my remarks.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

I had not really intended to inflict any remarks on the committee in connection with the minister's estimates on my own account, but my hon. friend, the member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, is unfortunately not able to be here today, and there are one or two matters which he wished to bring forward and which I am sure the minister will excuse me for bringing forward in his stead.
Before I do so, however, although I was not in the committee this morning I understand that an hon. gentleman on the other side of the house had some observations to make about the president of the Canadian National Railways, and I wish to say that so far as I am concerned-and I hope I am speaking in a completely non-partisan way- there have been times in the past 21 years or more of our friendship when Mr. Gordon and I have not seen eye to eye on some subjects. It is very hard for anyone with the strong opinions I have and the strong opinions Mr. Gordon has to always agree on everything, but he is in my opinion one of the greatest public servants this country has ever had.
Hear, hear.

Indeed, none of us who lived in Ottawa through those awful six years of war under the great strains which we experienced during that period will ever forget the extent to which Mr. Gordon's work enabled this country to make the tremendous effort it did at that time in the prosecution of our part of the war. Mr. Gordon undertook his present position without any previous experience in connection with railways, and I think no one would doubt that he undertook that task with the same zeal, the same energy and the same intelligence-and I might say the same disinterested patriotism-which he brought to every other task he ever undertook.
While many of us may disagree with some of his decisions at times, and there are

Supply-Transport
times when I have myself disagreed with them, I still believe no one could find grounds for questioning the disinterested public service of this great public servant.
The two matters which I wish to raise on behalf of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador are rather closely related and have to do with communications in Labrador. The first matter is one with which I know the minister's department is familiar, though he himself may not be familiar with it, and I am not asking him for his comments at this time but I just wish to place the matter on record and ask for his careful consideration of it. I would refer to an agreement made by the Department of Public Works, although today this is really a matter for the Department of Transport. The other party to the agreement was the Gulf of St. Lawrence Telephone Company, and it was made a short time before confederation, or at least what I call confederation, that is to say March 31, 1949.
If the minister will look up this agreement he will see that in so far as the operation of that company in the province of Quebec was concerned, there were certain stipulations about the maintenance of the service, and that similar stipulations were not made about the maintenance of the service in that part of Labrador which is in the province of Newfoundland. Of course it is easy to understand that at that time, since Newfoundland was not a part of Canada, it was not part of the domestic duty of the government of Canada to make provision with respect to that area, but it does seem to me that under the circumstances which have existed since March 31, 1949, there should have been protection and service given in Newfoundland equal to that given in Quebec. I am not going into the details of this matter, but I hope the minister will take a sympathetic look at the question, as I believe is the minister's practice in connection with all such matters.
The other matter to which I wish to refer is one which has always been directly under the minister's jurisdiction and, so the minister will not give me what used to be the stock answer though we are hearing it less and less, namely "Why didn't you do it", I will tell him right now why I didn't do it. It was because I was not able to persuade the minister's predecessor to do it; but I believe the arguments I put to that hon. gentleman in private are still sound arguments, and since I am not under the strain of the responsibility from which the present minister now suffers I can put those arguments in public at this time.
Under the terms of union, as the minister well knows, the telegraphic and telephonic
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
communications in Newfoundland were operated by the department concerned with postal and telegraphic communications in that province. In the island of Newfoundland these services were transferred to the Canadian National telegraph system, and that system has extended its service, not as fast as my friend the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and I would like to see it done, but it has been steadily extended. Unfortunately the same process did not apply in Labrador, although Labrador is just as much a part of the province of Newfoundland as is the island of Newfoundland. The facilities which then existed there were brought under the operation of the Department of Transport. Unhappily some of these facilities have been restricted in recent years, and there has been no expansion in Labrador comparable with that carried out by Canadian National Telegraphs on the island of Newfoundland. This has caused a great deal of inconvenience and some hardship and, in some cases, actual suffering in the area.
I know this is not a situation which could arise in any other part of Canada, because in other parts of this country telegraphic and telephonic communications are either provided by private companies or by provincial entities; but in the province of Newfoundland, because of its former status, the post office service was part of the postal and telegraphic department service. It is, in fact an inheritance from the days before confederation, and is one of those unique features which we have to take into account in our confederation in exactly the same way as in other respects we do with the province of Quebec.
I recognize that this is not a comparable situation at all, because I recognize how much more important is the situation from the point of view of Quebec. But in the same way that we respect the civil code of Quebec, this peculiar situation in the province of Newfoundland should be recognized and we should seriously consider maintaining, and where necessary expanding and improving, that service. I do hope these arguments which would have been made by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador had he been here will commend themselves to the minister.
I am now going to speak on my own account with respect to one other subject which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, and I hope that here again the minister will appreciate that I do not do so in a spirit of captious criticism.
I was very apprehensive when the minister told us in the house a month or so ago about this new policy of almost unrestricted competition which was being encouraged with regard to certain types of air service. We

are very apprehensive in Newfoundland- and I think the minister will probably find that this is true in other outlying areas-that this is going to result in fly by night competition-perhaps that is not a very happy image to use; I do not mean literally flying in the night time-but we are apprehensive lest outside companies should come in for a time, skim the cream off the milk, and then go out again.
