We know that this situation did exist in the thirties. We remember how some of these small companies, shoestring operators, were put out of business at that time. We think the minister should take another long and careful look at this matter and keep an eye on it to see that reputable companies which give service day and night, in season and out of season, are not going to And all the profit taken out of their flying by competition from operators who, once they have made a killing, will leave the place without any adequate service.
I have tried to speak to these points as briefly as possible. I would appreciate the minister's consideration of them.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, before addressing the house today on this subject, I think it would be timely for me to say something about my constituency. Saguenay is the biggest constituency in Canada, with the exception of the Northwest Territories. With an area of 374,000 square miles, it has a widely scattered population of approximately 80,000. There are 2,000 enfranchised Eskimos scattered among ten posts along James bay, Hudson bay and Ungava bay. The remainder of the population live in a 700-mile coastal strip along the St. Lawrence gulf and river, stretching from Tadoussac to Blanc Sablon.
Mr. Chairman, during my 8 years as director of the chamber of commerce of Baie Comeau, I had a firsthand opportunity of seeing that Saguenay's main economic obstacle is the dearth of adequate communication facilities, whether they be by air, land or sea.
Today, Mr. Chairman, I want particularly to mention our land transport facilities placing special emphasis on the necessity of a railroad on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. I shall try to be as concise as possible, as I do not wish to delay the progress of the session.
It has always been considered that the great thing in opening up an area is to build railroads; that is how the Canadian west was opened up-not, I would add parenthetically, without great sacrifices.
Supply-Transport
A railroad running from Great Slave lake is at present contemplated with a view to developing the mining industry.
Saguenay is going through a phase of full industrial expansion. Great strides are being made in the forestry and mining industries, and in power development.
I will name a few of the companies operating in my constituency: In forestry, we have the Quebec North Shore Paper, the Consolidated Paper Company, the Donnacona Paper, the Anglo Canadian Pulp and Paper, the St. Lawrence Corporation, the Canadian International Paper, and the Gulf Pulp and Paper.
As for mining, we have the Iron Ore Company of Canada, the Quebec Iron and Titanium Corporation, the Quebec Cartier Mining, and the Canadian British Aluminum. Further, Cyrus Eaton has a mammoth project for the development of the Hamilton Falls.
The grain elevators, I might add, are in the process of construction.
A 350-mile railway, the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway, built and financed by the Iron Ore Company, carries the ore from Knob Lake to Seven Islands. Another railroad is being laid down by Quebec Cartier Mining. It will stretch 150 miles from Shelter Bay, in the north of Quebec.
Even greater industrial expansion is foreshadowed in Saguenay by its enormous hydraulic resources. Saguenay's hydro-electric potential is calculated at 12 million horsepower.
To sum up, Mr. Chairman, we can say that the various companies have invested capital of at least a billion dollars so far, and economists assure us that, by 1970, companies' investments in Saguenay will exceed two billions.
It will be noted that the various companies operating in the Saguenay did not allow the constituency's development to be contingent upon federal aid in transport; these private undertakings went ahead with their own capital to build harbours, airports and railroads.
But I think, Mr. Chairman, that it is now up to the federal government to show its good will by improving our transport facilities. Indeed, the companies in Saguenay are confronted with a serious problem, namely, winter transport. Navigation in winter has become most difficult, regardless of all the aid from the federal government.
Consequently, heavy industry is forced to stockpile an enormous amount both of its production and of material needed for production. The same problem applies to small industry and trade. Businessmen must accordingly invest considerable amounts in the fall, so as to have the necessary material on hand for the winter.

Supply-Transport
Mr. Chairman, there is only one adequate solution to our transport problems, and that is to build a railroad from Seven Islands to Quebec. But I know that a responsible government must be sure that such a project will be self-liquidating before it can contemplate the enormous investments required for railroad construction.
In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I would draw special attention to the excellent brief submitted by the chamber of commerce of Baie Comeau to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects.
This brief contains all the necessary information to prove conclusively that not only would a railroad in Saguenay be a good proposition, but that it should also compensate for some of the deficits which the Canadian National Railways have in other areas.
In conclusion, I would like to quote an extract from this brief.
(Text):
An active and insistent group with the formidable title of "Comite du Chemin de Fer Chambre de Commerce du District de Baie Comeau" have been making studies of the possible rail routes and have met with Mr. Marler recently on this subject. We will quote the extracts from the report of our committee drawn up November 5, 1955. Certainly the question of the construction and economic prospects for a railway along the north shore should be given serious and immediate study by our federal government. Such a railway line, we believe, would be of national value to our great dominion with its growing importance, responsibilities and new sources of danger.
Our committee reports as follows: In view of the growth which is taking place in this section of the Saguenay and north shore region and the wealth of potential resources available for future development, it is important that consideration be given to supplying year-round transportation facilities in the form of a railroad.
While it is impossible for us to provide estimates of the present profitability of a railway line, joining present C.N.R. facilities and extending to Baie Comeau and Seven Islands, it is apparent such a rail line should be built in the general interest of Canada. We believe that there is sufficient assurance of future development in this area to merit such action.
...Any railroad can only be profitable if the freight traffic to warrant its construction and operation is available. The Minister of Transport mentioned a minimum of 500,000 tons a year would be required to warrant such a venture. Our committee is presently working on preliminary estimates and these are not yet complete; however, the first large item which we would be certain of is the movement of at least 100,000 cords of railed pulpwood which amounts to 250,000 tons to start with. There is merchandise, construction supplies and equipment, pulp and paper machinery and products, mining machinery and products, army, navy and air force requirements. With a population of 100,000 people, which we will realize in a very short time, and rapid and increasing flow of raw and manufactured or semi-manufactured materials, we believe the north shore and Labrador will load much more freight on a railway each year than you Will
[Mr. LaRue.j
find on some of the railways above enumerated which have been recently undertaken by the C.N.R. We count on your commission to draw to the attention of our government the need for ah immediate and serious study of our railway problem.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few matters I should like to bring to the attention of the minister at this time, and I do so in the knowledge that the Department of Transport which administers the Canadian National Railways has a great responsibility in the province of Newfoundland because the C.N.R. is practically our sole means of transportation there. Consequently I should like to bring a few points pertaining to transportation, particularly as they apply to the C.N.R., to the attention of the minister.
We all welcomed the announcement made by the minister to the effect that the long awaited arrival of the ferry William Carson was now an accomplished fact and that she had sailed into Port aux Basques harbour on a trial run. I do not intend to comment on this controversial vessel. All I should like to say is that I hope the minister later on in this discussion of his estimates will be able to tell the committee what are the results of that trial run, and also when the William Carson will be able to operate to Port aux Basques as she was intended.
During the time when further repairs and alterations were being made at Port aux Basques this vessel plied between North Sydney, Nova Scotia, and Argentia in the eastern part of Newfoundland. This fact lends emphasis to the following important point. As yet the province of Newfoundland does not have an adequate system of roads. No doubt some hon. members will be surprised to learn that it is impossible to drive from east to west in Newfoundland. Therefore the following question naturally arises. With the advent of this automobile ferry service to Port aux Basques, what useful purpose will it serve? I submit it will be many years before this vessel can operate as she was intended to operate, carrying automobiles from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland, because if she does go to Port aux Basques there are virtually no highways to take the automobiles across the province.
With that in mind I should like to point out the need for a ferry to ply between the eastern part of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia on the mainland of Canada. The Avalon peninsula is practically an island in itself. Two-thirds of the population of Newfoundland are domiciled there, and much of the industry in that

province is located there. Indeed, there is a great need for some means of communication between this peninsula and the province of Nova Scotia, in order that our people may communicate directly and freely with the rest of Canada.
I would hope that the minister, his department and particularly the Canadian National Railways will give consideration to the following request. If it proves that the William Carson cannot operate effectively to Port aux Basques, I hope consideration will be given to providing facilities at Argentia in the Avalon peninsula of Newfoundland so the vessel could operate as a car ferry to the eastern part of the province.
I have been concerned about the attitude of the C.N.R. with regard to Newfoundland, because whenever hon. members of this house representing Newfoundland have approached the Department of Transport or the railway concerning badly needed improvements they have been met with the attitude that such improvements would not be profitable. I submit it should not be a question of profit. The C.N.R. is the only means of transportation on the island of Newfoundland; consequently I believe it has a grave responsibility to the people of that province. Profit should be only a secondary consideration, and service should be placed above all else.
I noted with interest the comments of the minister to the effect that provision was made in his estimates for the construction of an auto ferry to ply between Portugal Cove and Bell island in my constituency. This is a very important island in the province of Newfoundland which for many years has carried on under a most inadequate system of transportation. Frequently the ferry service as it presently exists did not function at all.
When this new boat is put into operation I would ask the minister and his deputy to give consideration to extending Canadian National express services to Bell island. That island has a population of approximately 10,000 people and is the site of a great iron ore mine, one of Newfoundlands chief industries. The people there should have the benefit of Canadian National express service. At the present time they are treated the same as the residents of the city of St. John's, and they operate under the same regulations. If a Bell island businessman or resident receives goods via Canadian National express he has only 48 hours to go
Supply-Transport
to the express office in St. John's and claim his goods. If he does not reach the office within that period he is penalized. On the surface it would appear a simple matter, but for a resident of Bell island to reach St. John's he must cross a stretch of water which consumes 30 minutes of his time. In all about an hour is required to make the trip because the present ferry service does not operate on schedule.
Representations have been made to the department and to the railway on this important subject. I ask the minister to bring pressure to bear on the C.N.R. with a view to seeing whether it is feasible to establish a suboffice of the Canadian National express on Bell island so the local people will have the same advantages that are enjoyed by people in St. John's.
The other point I should like to make has to do with Torbay airport. A new terminal building is currently under construction there, and I understand that the official opening will possibly take place next month. In that connection I would emphasize the need for an alternate air strip. Torbay airport was built during the war as a military air field, and I am afraid very little consideration was given to the location of that air strip because flying conditions there are not always what they should be. As a matter of fact Torbay airport is closed in a lot more than it should be. About 30 or 35 miles from the site of the present airport at Torbay excellent flying conditions can be found, and the terrain lends itself to the building of an alternate air strip.
This is very important in view of the importance to my province, and to the city of St. John's particularly, of Trans-Canada Air Lines. With no road system so people can drive their cars across the province, and with no car ferry on which to put their cars in order to go to Nova Scotia, the people are practically wholly dependent on Trans-Canada Air Lines. Consequently it is a very serious handicap when Torbay airport is closed in for as much as a week at a time, as it sometimes is. I would ask the minister to give this matter serious consideration.
Finally, I should like to express my gratitude to the Minister of Transport for the great personal interest he has taken in matters pertaining to my province. There are many accomplishments which can be directly attributed to the minister, not the least of which is the building of the new car ferry for Bell

Supply-Transport
island. I hope his record will continue to be one of good service to the province of Newfoundland, and I hope the recommendations I have made this afternoon will merit his consideration.

The minister's introductory statement, which he made last night, contained two paragraphs which were devoted to the question of pilotage. I note that he said:
We expect in the coming months to send a special team of officials to our pilotage districts to hold discussions with the pilots themselves and other interested parties or groups in an effort to ensure that existing problems are not overlooked, and that we are doing our best to provide a proper atmosphere for the operation of pilotage.
The question immediately comes to my mind, why did the minister not do this long ago? We have had a dispute on the lakes -I know it appears a small matter affecting the livelihood of only some 40 Canadians- but why was this step not taken some time ago? However, he went on in his statement:
Special problems relating to the Kingston and the great lakes area will involve further discussions with the United States, as a result of construction of the seaway. At the moment, our objective is to provide a balanced framework within which pilotage may operate in the mutual interest of both shipping and pilots. Pilotage dues now represent a substantial cost to shipping-
I think we need to interpolate right here that pilotage dues do not represent a substantial cost to United States or Canadian ships within the great lakes system. I doubt very much that pilotage dues represent a substantial cost, because if you divide the cost of pilotage into the total tonnage carried by foreign ships I do not believe you would find it a terrific burden. Then the minister went on:
-and we will seek to avoid a situation in which this becomes so expensive as to injure shipping itself while, at the same time, ensuring the proper standard of working conditions for pilots.
When we were considering these estimates in the standing committee, the minister was very blunt in answering some points I tried to make. As a matter of fact he received considerable applause from most of the government members on that committee when he came out with the forthright statement that we did not care what the United States thought about this, Canada was going to set its pilotage policy on its own. I can certainly understand why the minister made that statement in the particular way he did, but it seems to me it overlooks, in its sharpness, the realities of the situation, because the minister in his statement said it involves further discussions with the United States. The minister's answer in the committee ignored the fact we have to co-operate with the United States just as they have to cooperate with us. There can be no throat-slitting by either party in this regard.
Supply-Transport
As I interpret the situation, it seems we have a lock-out or a strike, whatever you want to call it, and some 40 Canadian pilots who formerly made their living by piloting foreign ships in great lakes waters are out of work. Most of these pilots picked up their ships around Kingston and went on from there. As of last year they dealt with the shipping federation of Canada on a sort of temporary basis. The shipping federation of Canada is not a federation of Canadian shipping interests, it is really a committee representing foreign ship owners. The pilots formed themselves into an association and made arrangements with the United States association or union representing the masters and mates, to approach the whole seaway problem together from the pilots' point of view.
When it came time to renew the contract for this year with the shipping federation of Canada, the shipping federation turned down any negotiations on the demands of the pilots and informed them they were going to set up their own pilotage district between Port Weller and Sarnia. The shipping federation said they would not need pilots on any other part of the great lakes system. The deputy minister of transport, I understand, informed the shipping federation of Canada that it had no authority to set up a pilotage district and tried, along with the minister, to bring the shipping federation and the pilots together in some sort of colloquy to settle their problems.
The pilots have informed me that they have always been willing to go to such a meeting, either under the aegis of the minister now before us or the Minister of Labour. The shipping federation has refused to deal with this particular case. I have asked to have tabled the correspondence between the department and the shipping federation and with the dominion marine association, which is the third interested group. I had hoped to have that correspondence available today so I would have a better idea of the opinions exchanged between the ministry and these organizations.
The Canadian pilots had hopes that legislation which was passed by the United States House of Representatives and was before the Senate would win them back their jobs. It was expected that this legislation would become effective this fall. During what I understand was the last committee meeting to be held on this particular legislation the chairman of the committee, Senator Magnuson, announced that the state department, which

Supply-Transport
interposed no objection during the house consideration, telephoned him to urge delay because of opposition by the Canadian government.
In effect, therefore, this is one example where a Canadian protest had some result, unlike the Premium Iron Ores case where the Canadian protest seems to have been ignored. Our government, acting on the advice of the Minister of Transport, has blocked some United States legislation which indirectly would have had a beneficent effect on our own pilots; that is the way I interpret it. Perhaps I interpret it wrongly. I know that was not the consideration in the mind of the minister. I think he was undoubtedly pressing the point of view of the Canadian shipping federation, perhaps not deliberately because I suppose they are coincidental, with the emphasis upon the high cost of pilotage which may put tremendous burdens upon transportation costs and upset our whole dream of cheap shipping through having foreign bottoms come into the great lakes.
This is all very well as an argument, but we have to consider what is going to happen to Canadian shipping and Canadian pilots in this regard. What were the reasons for the anxiety of the United States, especially the United States coastguard, to go ahead with this particular bill, which the Canadian government managed to hold up temporarily? The emphasis in the United States bill was, I know, on safety and security and to have on foreign ships at all times in this very expensive seaway system pilots who had been screened both for ability and for loyalty.
As a result of the Canadian government's action in killing this bill, there are a couple of other possibilities looming up. One possibility is that each individual state along the great lakes will be able to write its own legislation so far as pilotage is concerned. We could get into a situation where Governor Harriman in New York could require a Canadian pilot to get off a ship going through that part of the canal and a United States pilot would take the ship through until it got back into the river. We know that sort of thing is probably nonsense, but the point I want to emphasize is that each of the states has retaliatory power if it wants to use it.
I underline the fact that we need an agreement with the United States on the federal level which will take all these factors into consideration. What I am afraid of is that the government, in its present ignorance, is going to be pushing strongly the interests of foreign shipping rather than, let us say, the interests of our Canadian pilots and the mutual interest they have with the United

States pilots. I feel also that the government may be missing the safety factor.
I should like to read to the committee, Mr. Chairman, part of a statement by Captain John Bishop, international secretary treasurer of the international organization of masters, mates and pilots, in support of this bill No. S-2096 of the United States House of Representatives, which was blocked in the Senate by our government's action. I read this in order not to back up his position completely but just to put on record the American side of opinions, which opinions are held by our great lakes pilots and held with sincerity. Captain Bishop said:
I am appearing today in support of S-2906, a bill which would upon enactment, formulate a long-needed safety factor in the fast growing navigation program in the great lakes and St. Lawrence seaway area.
The present laws regarding manning by licensed officers on United States and Canadian vessels provides for sufficient qualified personnel, licensed by the appropriate agency of the countries mentioned. However, the fact remains that foreign vessels are not required by law to provide for competent and qualified personnel to pilot their vessels in the area under consideration and covered by the provisions of this bill. The fact that this situation exists, certainly indicates that no matter how proficient and qualified the American or Canadian pilot may be in the execution of his duties, complications will arise over which he has no control.
It may be readily seen that a hazardous situation will exist when, during each such an ordinary event as the passing of two vessels, where one being piloted by a thoroughly competent licensed pilot and the other is manned with a crew of individuals who may be making their first trip in the great lakes area and are unfamiliar with our passing signals, rules and regulations. There are even cases when communication by radiotelephone is impossible, due to the language barrier between the foreign crew or the American or Canadian crew.
Although the passenger vessel trade is small in nature as compared to the bulk and dry cargo trade on the lakes, one major catastrophe caused by the lack of properly experienced pilot personnel would prove tremendously embarrassing to the opponents of this legislation as well as a possible reflection of dereliction of duty on those charged with the safeguarding of the American public.
The reciprocal feature of the bill involving Canada provides the solution to any possible problem which may arise due to the geographic nature of the ports and channels of the seaway and the ports in the great lakes area.
The significance of proper pilotage regulation can be best indicated by the fact that in practically every seaport in the world, a pilot native to that country is required by law on entering or leaving the port or navigating in canals, rivers or other areas which may be deemed dangerous.
In other words, if I may interject here, if a Canadian ship goes into foreign ports it is going to have to have a pilot in almost every case. But we are much more generous with

our ports and our installations, at least in this government's view. Captain Bishop goes on to say:
I think the record of casualties involving vessels without the proper personnel will indicate the necessity for regulation of vessels covered by this proposed legislation.
In the interest of marine safety, it is essential that a pilot or other qualified officer direct and control vessels navigating on certain channels and rivers of the great lakes system. We further maintain that when a vessel is in the open areas of the great lakes, it would be sufficient if the pilot was on board subject to call to assume control and direct the navigation of the vessel.
One fact which we feel of equal importance is the feature of security which would be provided by the enactment of S-2096. Although the presence of an American or Canadian officer would not by any stretch of imagination stop any smuggling of contraband or narcotics into this country we feel it would be a factor which would at least slow it down, also the illegal entry of aliens could be more closely observed and reported to the proper authority.
The American officer at the present time must be screened by the United States coastguard for security and loyalty wherein a great deficiency exists on foreign flag vessels in this respect.
The safety factor for American shipping alone warrants the endorsement and support of this organization.
That statement is the United States pilots' position. In other words, they insist that safety and security are extremely important there. Our government evidently feel that those matters are not major considerations. I understand that the United States coastguard helped to prepare the bill which our government blocked. We must assume that the United States coastguard considered safety and security to be extremely important matters.
I know we must balance safety and security against cost. I should like the minister to tell us just what pilotage costs are in relation to the total costs of moving freight in the great lakes. One of the points I think the minister must recognize, if he knows anything about foreign ships, is that they work with practically skeleton crews compared with our own lake ships. There were foreign ships on the lakes this summer with crews as small as 10 or 11 men. Yet the minister is worried about the cost of pilotage of these ships, and evidently seems willing to present the point of view of this group of foreign ship owners that the high costs of pilotage are something about which we need to be deeply concerned.
There is one final point I wanted to make in connection with this matter. This is from a brief prepared by the great lakes pilot association, which states as follows:
The shipping federation argues that pilots are not needed on "the open waters" of the great lakes. Foreign ships propose to use-and they are now using-pilots in the Welland canal, the Detroit river and the St. Clair river. They state that they do not even wish to use pilots on lake Erie.

The argument is completely fallacious. The so-called "open waters" can be and often are very dangerous. There are many hazards in shallow lake Erie.
On all the lakes fog or snow can and frequently do reduce visibility. In bad weather ships are required to give many signals. Foreign shipmasters persistently give the wrong signals, not being familiar with the inland shipping rules. One foreign master, on a voyage from Toronto to Kingston early in May, 1958, admitted that he did not even have a copy of the inland rules in his possession. He, however, had been wise enough to take on a pilot at Toronto (contrary to the instructions of the federation) and was able to proceed to Kingston in heavy fog without mishap.
I understand that the departmental officials are ready to go into consultation with their United States counterparts to thresh out legislation which I understand the government is considering bringing in next session, and which one would understand the United States congress would pass some time next year. Their session starts in January. Probably it would become law by the middle of next summer. In other words, in the next few months there is to be a threshing out of this whole problem on an interdepartmental basis between Canada and United States officials.
I should like to suggest to the minister that in these discussions his officials take a bit more broadminded look at the proposals the Americans have than he seems to have indicated in his reply in committee. I sincerely believe that the arguments of the pilots' association, as far as security and safety are concerned, are extremely important. The arguments that he put so strongly and the propaganda the ship owners put so strongly, namely this whole idea of "feather-bunking" and "we are not having the United States union dictate our set-up in Canada", I think are rather emotional arguments that are advanced by people who do not have a very sound position.
I should like the minister to look into the matter personally just in order to see how powerful a factor the pilotage costs are in the total cost of materials being moved on this great lakes seaway. I should like to have some idea in terms both of percentage of the cost and also percentage of the cost in relation to wages that are paid on the ships that are moving the material.
In conclusion on this particular point may I say this. The United States coastguard has a rather remarkable reputation that has been improving, I would say, until it stands in many Americans' minds almost on a par with their practically worshipped United States marines. I do not know whether the United States coastguard is entitled to the high reputation it has, but if there is any merit at all in this high reputation then there must be a great deal of merit in the

Supply-Transport
proposals which have been made and which were embodied in that United States bill which our government has blocked. I would like the discussions to take place with a recognition on the part of this government that these men are not fools and that they do not resent this legislation which is nothing more than the backing up of the pettifogging of some United States unions, but that there is much more to it than that.

As I do not
wish to prolong this discussion, I will omit the usual congratulations to the minister because I will congratulate him at a later date. I just wish to introduce a subject which is not a matter with which he is altogether unfamiliar and this also applies to his deputy minister. Rather than going over the same old ground again, I hope to present a solution to what has become a most difficult problem, not for any particular region but for the whole of Canada.
I refer to what we normally call the bilateral agreement between Canada and the United States on air transportation routes. Until recently we have been one of those countries interested in the opening of bilateral negotiations but we now find ourselves in a position, particularly with respect to the United States of America, which involves matters which are the concern of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and the Department of External Affairs. Until the past few months it did look as though Canada and the United States were going to be able to sit down at something less than a summit conference to discuss how the international agreement has been affected by changed circumstances since it was amended in 1951 and the fact that there are areas in both countries which are not receiving the type of services which the various communities involved require.
As an example, in the city from which I come there is absolutely no north-south connection and we know that various congressmen and senators in the United States have been more than interested in seeing that a particular airline should be granted rights by the United States administration to land in Calgary but that we have run up against an impasse. This impasse does not constitute something peculiar to the present administration because it dates back almost 10 years, but neither government has been able to move ahead in connection with this agreement because of certain differences between them.
This is the past history and today we find ourselves in the situation where the United States, just as recently as a month ago, indicated they were prepared to re-negotiate
IMr. Fisher.]
the bilateral agreement between the two countries which we had hoped would eventually lead to better and a greater number of routes for both countries. We now find that there is an objection raised by the United States with respect to the landing of transports carrying immigrants from Europe to Canada and this objection has prevented the discussion of the agreement at the top level.
I want to suggest to the minister a solution. First of all, in the event that the United States continues to insist that this question of immigrants should hold up the discussion of the bilateral agreement, I suggest this is a matter which could be referred to the cabinet committees recently set up by Prime Minister Diefenbaker and President Eisenhower or, failing that, that the subject matter could be discussed by the proposed committee to be established between the legislatures of the two countries. I am suggesting that the question of immigration and where these immigrants are to be picked up and whether or not they are to first land in the United States and from there journey to Canada, is not a matter which should affect an international air agreement such as this one. I say this particularly in view of the fact that this agreement can help to a very large extent to develop air routes between the two countries.
If that suggestion is not acceptable I believe that if the United States and Canada still cannot come to any agreement because of this problem then it is in the interests of Canada to permit unilateral discussions to take place. I believe that it does not perhaps require a formal agreement between our countries, but perhaps could be dealt with on a purely limited basis involving, for instance, an amendment to the charter to provide Canada with landing rights for a particular airline which I have mentioned, so that it may utilize the facilities in the city of Calgary which, as I have said, is completely without a north-south connection. I realize that this presents difficulties and I have now reduced it to a local rather than a national problem, but I am sure that those who have travelled across Canada will agree with me when I say that when one considers any Canadian city having a population of over a quarter of a million people, when one considers our citizens are not permitted the advantage of a direct route for flights to the United States, when one considers the centre of the petroleum industry which has one company alone making 235 flights a year for which it must operate its own airline, he has to realize the urgency which, although admittedly it has existed for six years, is becoming more extreme every day.
I am not speaking of any particular government but refer to the governments of

both countries when I say it is time we should stop hiding behind what has really become a technicality which is preventing us from carrying on these discussions. When I have broached the subject to the minister or to his deputy I have received nothing but courtesy, but I am reaching the point where I believe the discussions are going to have to take place. These considerations preventing us from re-opening negotiations on this bilateral agreement must be dealt with entirely separately and the question of immigration particularly should be considered on its own merits. I do hope the minister will find an opportunity to reply to this suggestion.

Living as I do at the top
of the Niagara escarpment at the site of the twin locks of the Welland ship canal, I have had more to do with the Department of Transport than with any other department of government. Like the hon. member for Laurier I congratulate the minister on his appointment to one of the most important, and I think the most interesting, government portfolios, and I would also pay tribute to the officers and employees in his department who have always given to me and to my problems every consideration.
I think the minister is doing a very good job and I have never thought he was overstaffed except perhaps at one time, and that was during last March, when I thought at least in my area there were more employees on the Welland canal, or there seemed to be more employees there, than there were shovels or tools for them to use. However, that situation was soon corrected and I hope the minister will still take the same keen interest in the number of unemployed in my area as he showed at that time.
The ministers of transport have always taken great interest in the Welland ship canal. At the time of my first election the hon. member for Laurier, who was then minister of transport, came to my constituency and later the Hon. Mr. Marler was down there and at the last election the present minister showed up there.

I would think that probably this is an invitation to members on this side at least to go over his estimates with a fine tooth comb on this particularly occasion and to give his department more than just passing attention. He also told an audience in Welland that if they would only elect a Tory candidate that he would tell him when he came here what he would do about the overhead crossings across the Welland canal. I know the minister is honest, and that he had no plans about the crossings over the canal, because on the orders of the day I have asked him about them since and he has admitted that he has had no communications from the minister of highways of Ontario about building bridges over the canal. When Premier Frost announced the planning of the construction of three toll bridges across the canal the minister seemed to be just as surprised as I was at that particular time. I hope the minister will not further try to dispense with me in this parliament. I have not much to say and very little criticism to make of his department. '
I regret indeed to see the Department of Transport handing over the operation of the canal to the St. Lawrence seaway authority. These canals have always been operated with efficiency by the Department of Transport and I know that the employees of the Welland ship canal at least will not hail these changes with any degree of satisfaction. I hope that these efficient, trustworthy and loyal employees will be remembered and that they will continue to have their seniority and pension rights.
In connection with the approaches to the canal crossings at Welland, Port Colborne and other centres of population there is much annoyance and inconvenience caused by the holding up of traffic. This applies also on the Queen Elizabeth way. I hope the minister will give every co-operation to the department of highways of Ontario with respect to the problem of the congestion at these bridges and their approaches.
The agreement between this government and the municipalities of St. Catharines, Mer-ritton and Thorold regarding the old Welland canal rehabilitation and clean-up has been finalized and I would like to ask the minister when this work will get under way. There are a good many unemployed in this area, and if the minister would only co-operate I could send him many men to help along with this work.
The hon. member for Port Arthur brought up the question of the dispute between the shipping federation of Canada and the great lakes pilots association over the use of pilots on ocean-going boats in our great lakes system. I have received many letters from people interested in this and I was glad to

Supply-Transport
hear the minister say he would send somebody down to contact the pilots and other people who are interested. I note that the department has no present authority to require pilots on boats on the great lakes system and that it has informed the shipping federation that it could arrange, or had the right to arrange, for pilotage on its own behalf for ships of its members in the area from Port Weller to Sarnia. There was one statement that the department did not want to give the impression that this was a scheme approved by the department.
I should like to ask the minister if he has evolved any scheme to deal with this. I should also like to ask him if in his own words of July 1st it is his conviction and the conviction of the department that to impose pilotage fees upon shippers where pilots are not necessary-and I take it he thinks they are not necessary in the open lakes- amounts to imposing an extra and unnecessary burden on shipping charges generally which must be borne eventually by the consuming public. I should like to ask the minister, also, if the masters who are piloting ships of the shipping federation of Canada from Port Weller to Sarnia and back are fully qualified. I should further like to ask the minister if the communication system belonging to the Department of Transport on the Welland ship canal is being utilized by the ships to contact pilots other than those belonging to the great lakes pilots association.
The pilots of this association are well trained and responsible men and I understand that they hold certificates from the Department of Transport. I should like to see the Department of Transport try to compose the differences between these pilots, their association and the foreign ships.
I hope the department can arrange some satisfactory agreement because these men are well trained. They are experts and they have been off work most of the summer. I suppose we may expect some legislation at the next session of parliament if similar legislation goes through congress and I can say here that the pilots themselves think that this government is taking the side of the shipping federation of Canada. I do not know whether that is so or not; I am just saying that that is their impression.
There are two other questions I should like to ask the minister at this time. Will the St. Lawrence seaway and the Welland ship canal be turned over to the St. Lawrence seaway authority by order in council, and has any action been taken in this regard. I should also like to ask a question in connection with tolls. I notice that the hon. member for Lincoln brought up the matter of

tolls and said he was against tolls on the Welland canal. I have often spoken in this house on the same subject, expressing myself against tolls on the Welland ship canal. However, it seems likely that tolls will be applied. That is the last information I have been able to obtain. In these circumstances I should like to know if these tolls will be applied by order in council or if they will be brought before parliament so that we may have a chance to discuss them next year before the opening of navigation.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join other hon. members who have offered congratulations to the minister on the efficiency of his department and on the very fair attitude which his officials have taken with regard to questions of local interest which are brought before him.
I should like to say a few words this afternoon on the subject of some of the facilities maintained by the department in the Montreal area. I was very happy to hear the minister's statement this morning with regard to air conditioning at Montreal airport in reply to a question by the hon. member for Cartier. The minister will remember that I, along with others, spoke to him privately about this matter, and we are very glad to hear that further consideration is to be given to it. Of course, we hope that results will be favourable for the airport.
The Montreal research council, which is a body sponsored by McGill University, has made a very thorough investigation and brought out a report concerning the impact of the St. Lawrence seaway on the Montreal area. I am sure the minister and his officials have received copies of this report and no doubt have studied the recommendations made but I should like to place some of the recommendations on the record at this time because with the opening of the seaway which is imminent will come a time of crisis for the port of Montreal. Since Canada became an active trading nation the port of Montreal has been the most important port in the country and the effect of the seaway on this port will depend to a large extent on how well plans have been laid by the federal, provincial and civic governments. I do not wish to dwell at great length on the detail of how these recommendations were arrived at but I should like to emphasize to hon. members that the group that made the investigation was a large one and took a considerable amount of time in conducting the study. The recommendations of that body are well worth consideration by the department where they apply to the federal government.

I should like first to read from some of the general conclusions contained in the report:
Stripped of qualifications and refinements, this study suggests that the seaway is likely to confer substantial economic benefits on the Montreal area's traffic in grain, coal and iron ore; that little or no change is to be expected in the volume of local petroleum traffic; that the port may well incur significant losses in general cargo business handled; and that the seaway stimulus to industrial location in Montreal is not likely to be of major proportions. In short, the local pattern for the future is a mixed one, precluding any simple estimate of net seaway effect.
It is pointed out in the paragraph above that there is an expectation of increased grain traffic and the department has already instituted some of the improvements in the grain facilities in Montreal that will be required. I should like now to turn to the subject of ore. The section on ore contains the following conclusion:
The post-seaway outlook presents difficulties, however. Any substantial rise in local tonnage of imported ore will be contingent, to a considerable extent, on the expansion of Montreal's handling facilities. While existing dock space, water depth and storage capacity are generally quite adequate for future needs, this is not so in the case of the rate of discharge. And the problem here will be further accentuated when transshipment is made directly into upper lakers with a carrying capacity roughly equal to that of the ocean ore vessels. In short, the greatest priority attaches to those improvements which will increase the speed of turn-round of bulk carriers in Montreal harbour.
As I mentioned when reading the general conclusions, general cargo is the field in which Montreal must expect to lose. General cargo, of course, is that part of the port business that provides the greatest proportion of employment. The amount of general cargo we will lose will be dependent on the facilities available in the harbour. I should like to quote the conclusion contained in the report in regard to general cargo facilities:
In common with most established ports, however, the bulk of Montreal's facilities were constructed many years ago, and consequently, under present-day conditions, considerable strain on these facilities is apparent. The trucking industry, for example, complains of serious traffic congestion on the harbour front, and of antiquated transit sheds which do not permit the most efficient handling of goods.
And further:
It should be added that improvement of these general cargo facilities is currently under way in Montreal. For example, the federal government is building four transit sheds which will extend the port's shed floor area by nearly 300,000 square feet. However, there would appear to be a substantial need for further expansion and improvement of general cargo facilities in the Montreal area.
In common with other hon. members of the committee from the Montreal area I am extremely concerned that everything possible be done so that in those areas where Montreal may expect to be hurt by the opening of the
Supply-Transport
seaway the impact shall be as minor as possible and therefore I wanted to read these recommendations into the record for the consideration of the minister and his officials.
I should like to add an additional thought in connection with traffic in the area of the Montreal harbour which is a very congested area. With the developing trend of shipping by truck rather than by railroad the port will be at a great disadvantage if there is not a great improvement in the traffic situation in and around the harbour so that trucking firms will be willing at reasonable rates to take on cargo from shipping in the harbour. I realize that for the most part this problem is a civic one. Nevertheless there is a considerable mileage of roads in that area under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. The suggestion has been made that a through-way established along the harbour front which would in part pass over the national harbours' board property would be of great advantage. I hope that in consultation with the civic authorities there the department will give sympathetic consideration to co-operation both with regard to allowing use of the department's land and with regard to financing with a view to providing a modern highway system in that area so that not only private cars but more particularly trucking facilities can get in and out of the harbour area quickly and with a minimum of delay.

Mr. Chairman, on August 15 last, following a report which appeared in the Star of August 13 and another report which appeared on August 14, I directed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) as to whether air conditioning would be provided at the new Dorval airport. I was very glad to hear the hon. minister this morning inform the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) that he would take into serious consideration the representations made and that he would soon make another statement in the house, which, if I understood him well, would satisfy everybody. I am very happy to see that the minister has decided to reconsider his decision and I sincerely hope that he will see fit to go ahead with and put in air conditioning in that important building.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I come to another subject with which I have often dealt in this house, that is the provision of adequate protection at level crossings throughout the country.
On June 28, 1955, parliament enacted an amendment to the Railway Act to allow the

Supply-Transport
federal government to contribute 60 per cent of the cost of construction of adequate protection at level crossings, up to a maximum of $300,000. This year the federal government has decided to amend again this act and raise its contribution to 80 per cent, up to a maximum of $500,000. It is another step in the right direction.
When we think of the number of lives lost throughout the country because of inadequate protection at level crossings, we realize that the expenses necessary to ensure adequate protection at such crossings are insignificant. Taking into account the number of lives lost and the money spent each year to protect human lives, prevent accidents and safeguard the health of Canadians, I believe that the amounts spent for the protection of people at level crossings are not wasted.
If we think also about the difficult situation in which the municipalities have found themselves these last years on account of the expenses they incurred in connection with level crossings, we must realize that the federal government, as well as the provincial governments, must do something to help them.
Both during the last electoral campaign and the preceding one, a promise was made that the federal, provincial and municipal authorities would be brought into a conference with a view to helping our municipalities. That is another promise which the Conservative government has not yet fulfilled. However, the fact that this government intends to help the municipalities by paying 80 per cent of the cost of construction of means of protection at level crossings is something that will help the municipalities.
Following my election as member for Dollard and during the first session, I had the opportunity of pointing out here that there were in the constituency of Dollard, and more particularly in Ville St. Laurent, several railway crossings about which the federal government should do something in order to protect human lives. In some cases, I met with some success. I shall mention only one, because during the last election campaign, the official Conservative candidate in the constituency of Dollard, his worship mayor Cousineau-and I hope this will not be too displeasing to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, Mr. Pigeon-had promised, in his electoral program, as published in the newspaper I'tcho de Dollard:
My dear friends,
The day of reckoning is at hand. It will then be time to decide who is going to represent us in Ottawa, in the forthcoming administration.

Briefly, I would favour, in addition to the articles of my party's platform, the following measures:
Among other things, Mr. Cousineau said:
Adequate protection at railway crossings in the constituency of Dollard.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I did not wait for the mayor of Ville St. Laurent, the Conservative candidate in the constituency of Dollard, to serve the people of my constituency and more particularly that of Ville St. Laurent. As I said a moment ago, at my first session here, I made representations to the then minister of transport, Mr. Chevrier, now member for Laurier, and in some cases I obtained the protection I was asking in regard to railway crossings.
In fact, on March 1, 1956, I received a letter from Mr. Henri A. Dore, chairman of the Property Owners' Association of Northeastern St. Laurent, in which he thanked me for the work I had done in order to obtain what I had asked, and I will quote only one passage:
Dear Sir,
The automatic signals at the railway crossing of Cote Vertu, in Ville St. Laurent, have been in operation since February 6 last, as you had forecast in your last letter.
Well, Mr. Chairman, it is certainly not the Conservative candidate who was running in the last election, who obtained that protection at the Cote Vertu railway crossing; in fact, it was done even before he decided to be a parliamentary candidate.

I thank hon. members of the committee for their consideration of this request under the unusual circumstances existing and I shall not detain the minister in the consideration of his estimates for more than a few moments in order to draw attention to the principal items which I should like hon. members to consider before the next session when it would be my hope the resolution might appear again under private members' notices of motion.
Understandably we are most concerned with the impact of the resolution upon eastern Canadian ports. We have some of the finest harbours in North America which are well served by both inland and ocean transportation lines. Particularly the ports of Halifax and Saint John represent the investment of many millions of dollars of federal money. That investment was originally made and has continued to grow in order to provide all Canada with an outlet to the sea from her eastern shores. It is well known that this investment in large part lies fallow during the season of navigation in the St. Lawrence river. We are understandably concerned about the future impact of the St. Lawrence seaway upon our area. It would be ideal if we could find a way to utilize the facilities of the east coast throughout the year. Because of the use of the ports for only a brief period of each year, we feel it is all the more important that the ports on the Atlantic shore should be utilized to the fullest extent during the four or five months of every year in which they are Canada's only ice-free outlets to the Atlantic ocean. But instead of this full utilization, Mr. Chairman, what do we find? We find that vast quantities of cargo are both exported and imported via United States ports. We find that hundreds of millions of dollars in inland transportation charges, in labour costs and in port service charges flow across the border yearly instead of staying in this country where they could contribute to the prosperity of all our people.
We in the Atlantic provinces are disturbed at this tremendous flow of Canadian foreign trade through non-Canadian channels. We do not, however, urge that all such traffic go through Canadian ports. We realize that our neighbours to the south possess some of the finest ports in the world and that, for a number of reasons, some of our traffic probably will always use their installations. However, we insist and urge that companies which derive their prosperity from the Canadian market make a special effort to ship both their import and export requirements through our Canadian ports. We in the Atlantic provinces are realistic enough to realize that 
patriotic sentiment is not the only or the most important business factor under normal conditions.
I will make one or two suggestions in a moment's time. In the interval I should like to point out the significance of the Atlantic ports to the regional economy of the area. Every ship that enters or leaves any port on the eastern coast of Canada, of course, provides jobs and dollars for our people. This is true also in the United States. Hon. members of the committee may not be aware of the fact that the port of New York authority has estimated that that great port supports one out of four of the 13 million people living in the area. We have no similar statistics relating to Halifax and Saint John but I doubt whether, if we did have them, they would differ greatly from the New York statistics.
Our ports provide a multitude of jobs in a variety of fields. The men who are actively engaged in all sorts of businesses, from those engaged in the handling of cargo such as freight handlers, stevedores, even down to banks and mercantile companies, benefit from port business. We have estimated that in the port of Halifax and the port of Saint John the annual wages of longshoremen, freight handlers, watchmen and checkers alone come to about $10 million. By the economic principle of "free economic generation", by which every dollar earned by these workers generates or creates two dollars of additional income, hon. members will see that this represents at least thirty million very valuable dollars to us.
I should like to ask the members of the committee during the interval, and perhaps before we have an opportunity to discuss the matter in a full day's debate at the next session, whether they would consider, in relation to the tables prepared by the national harbours board which they have kindly consented to have printed in Hansard, these possibilities as corrective devices. We believe that the utilization of Canadian ports could be vastly increased. We believe that it may be possible at next month's commonwealth trade talks to suggest to other commonwealth countries whether it would not be possible to implement something paralleling the British preferential tariff to apply to goods brought into Canada from commonwealth countries through Canadian ports. We think that perhaps we might urge commonwealth countries to allow the British preferential tariff only on such of their imports from Canada as have been shipped out via a Canadian port. There is certainly no doubt that the recapture of part of the nearly $400 million a year of Canadian trade passing through United States ports instead of through

Canadian ports would be of tremendous assistance not only to the ports of Halifax and Saint John and their people but to the entire economy of the Atlantic provinces and to that extent to the entire economy of the country.

I too, Mr. Chairman, should like to join with all those who have congratulated the minister on his appointment to the office, as this is the first appropriate occasion on which it could be done, and also on this first occasion of the presentation of his estimates before parliament.

I am sorry that the pressure of work has made it impossible for me to keep abreast of the evidence so I trust that the minister will bear with me if I raise a few questions as the various items of his estimates come before the committee.
There is probably no department of the federal government which touches the lives of the people of my province more intimately than does the Department of Transport. Newfoundland has seafaring traditions going back over 400 years; we are a seafaring people and a great part of the population spends a large part of their lives on the sea. In Newfoundland more than in any other province, the people are dependent upon the sea, either directly or indirectly, for their living. Furthermore, all of our necessities must be brought in by water because the majority of our population lives on the island of Newfoundland and practically everything we produce must be sold in world markets and therefore must be taken out by water. In no other province do the transportation costs play such a large part in the cost of living as they do in Newfoundland and for that reason we deplore the decline in our mercantile fleet.
There is need for special shipping to take care of the requirements of our province. This is the age of specialization and specialization must certainly be applied to Canadian shipping if we are to keep up with the times and to meet competition from other maritime countries. We need special ships to carry our fish particularly to the West Indies

markets. There is a need for a special selfunloading ship to bring coal into our province and this is one way in which the minister and his department could kill three birds with one shot. He could certainly help the shipbuilding industries and the coal mining industry in Nova Scotia and at the same time by lowering the cost of coal help the people of Newfoundland if his department would consider providing assistance for the construction of a self-unloading coal carrier. Then we need small ships of from 200 to 300 tons to distribute our goods from the large centres to the smaller fishing settlements in our province and there is a need for special assistance to encourage the industry to provide these ships. I do hope the minister and his department will give some consideration to this matter.
I would also like the minister to do whatever can be done to remove the restrictions in order to permit the importation of used trawlers for our fishing industry which can be obtained in other countries at a fraction of the price that would have to pay for them in Canada. Either the government must subsidize our own shipbuilding industry or some other means must be found so that these ships which are essential for the development of the fishing industry may be obtained without the outlay of too great a capital expenditure.
At this juncture I should like to say a few words about the Newfoundland railway. The function of any railway is to integrate the economy of the area it serves. In Newfoundland it has two functions because Newfoundland can be divided into three separate economic sectors. There is the Avalon peninsula which is almost an island, as the hon. member for St. John's East pointed out this afternoon; there is the western end of Newfoundland; and, in between, we have the central part of the island. Each of these divisions has a separate economy and one function of the railway is to integrate these separate divisions into a single provincial economy. But since Newfoundland is a part of Canada, the railroad has another function.

This could and should be done in such a way that no part of Newfoundland would be more than 24 hours away from the mainland. costs play so large a part in the cost of living as they do in Newfoundland and to support this contention by way of illustration I should like to quote a paragraph from an article which I have just discovered in the Sunday Herald dated August 31, 1958. This article speaks about a decision of the A and P chain stores not to set up branches in Newfoundland and it goes on to explain why.
The A and P officials said that on visiting Newfoundland they discovered that it was almost impossible to ship in perishable goods without the resultant loss being so large as to make the product too expensive to sell. They point out that fresh vegetables, for example, such as tomatoes, lettuce, arrive in their warehouses in Toronto or Montreal one day, and are shipped out direct to their own stores within a matter of 24 hours. In other words, all products are turned over in a 24-48 hour period.
If they were involved in Newfoundland, they pointed out to the Sunday Herald, it could be seven days from the time the products were shipped from their Montreal warehouse to the time they were received in St. John's stores, and this delay alone would result in tremendously increased overhead.
That illustrates very clearly the handicap under which the people of Newfoundland have to labour because of the difficulties in their transportation system and it also illustrates the handicap that businessmen must undergo in comparison with their mainland counterparts. Since Newfoundland is an island, everything must go in by water and because we do not have a rail car ferry we are precluded from buying in carload lots. A firm in Halifax can buy a carload of bananas or oranges from Florida and have them shipped almost to the door but a load ordered in Newfoundland has to go to North Sydney where it must be broken down, put on a ship, taken off again, put into another narrow gauge car, transported to its destination and then unloaded again. Moreover, goods brought in from central Canada have to be packaged as though they were intended for export and not only do we have to bear the cost of extra handling but we also have to pay extra packaging costs as well. That is a tremendous handicap and it is one which must some day be removed because it certainly cannot be allowed to continue indefinitely. I realize that this is a long term project because you cannot build a railway overnight. It is probably a 10-year project, but the time to start thinking about it is now, and I hope the minister will begin to give consideration to these matters which I have outlined.
There is one other point to which I want to bring the minister's attention in connection with the adjustment of freight claims for losses incurred on goods being carried by the railroad. As I understand it, if goods which are being carried by rail, or on the ferry

across the strait, which is part of the railway, should be lost in transit, any loss or damage that occurs is the subject of compensation by the railways. But the coastal steam service, which is not considered part of the railway, though it serves the same purpose as the railroad for those who are living around the coastline, is operated under a different system and a person to whom goods are consigned cannot enforce any claim should goods be lost in transit. I had a number of cases brought to my attention arising out of an accident in which a motor vessel ran aground in Placentia bay a year ago. As a result of that accident a large quantity of goods was damaged and when people sent in their claims to the claims division of the railway they were told: we cannot pay you anything because these ships are not part of the railway; they are just ordinary water carriers, and this was an act of God and the goods were carried subject to the conditions on the waybill. Therefore you have no claim. As a result, the people who live inland and who are served by the railway line are treated differently from those who live on the coast and who must depend on the coastal service which is the equivalent of the railway service in the coastal areas of Newfoundland. I hope the minister will look into this matter because it is important that the coastal boats should be considered part of the railway service in the same way as the ferry which crosses the gulf is considered to be.
My hon. friend from St. John's East referred to the William Carson this afternoon and I hope, as he does, that the minister will give us a full account of the recent trial runs. I hope, also, that he will find it possible to give us an exact breakdown of the cost of this ship, because so many stories have been told about the cost of this vessel that in the interest of telling the public the truth and setting the record straight I think this should be stated. If the minister cannot provide the figures at this moment perhaps he will be able to do so later on this evening, or tomorrow. I should like him to state exactly what the ship costs, what the terminals cost, what the harbour improvements cost and what the operating costs have been. My hon. friend from St. John's indicated that if the trial runs were not too successful this ship might be diverted to the ferry service between the mainland and Argentia.
I do not blame him for trying to get an improved service for his constituency. I would do the same thing if I were in his place. But I must point out to him-and I am sure the minister does not need to be reminded of this -that the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada expressly stated that this ship was built for service between North

Sydney and Port aux Basques and for nowhere else. The minister and the government are bound by that agreement and by the terms of union to maintain that ship in that service and to see it is not diverted anywhere else.
With regard to Argentia as a terminal, I would disagree with the hon. member for St. John's East that it is suitable for this purpose. Perhaps it is suitable from the standpoint of harbour facilities and from the standpoint of the Canadian National Railways but it is certainly most unsuitable from the standpoint of public convenience because Argentia is a United States naval base. One can enter and leave there only with the permission of the United States authorities. I have personally had the experience many times. When I went to join one of the C.N.R. ships I had to secure a pass to enter through the gateway before I could board the ship. That is not a satisfactory state of affairs from the public standpoint. Furthermore, there is no place at Argentia to erect a waiting room, a snack bar or any kind of facility for people who have to wait either for the ship to arrive or for a train to take them back to St. John's. It may happen that in ten years' time the United States will not be interested in Argentia and perhaps the lease will be cancelled but as long as the lease is in force Argentia is not a suitable place from the public standpoint for a terminal of the C.N.R.
I have one or two minutes left at my disposal and I wish to refer to the reorganization of the department about which the minister spoke in his opening remarks. I could not gather from what he said just how far the reorganization had extended but if it has not already done so I hope it will extend down to the marine districts. It happens that part of the coast of Newfoundland and part or perhaps all of the coast of Labrador come under the agency of Prince Edward Island. That may be convenient for the department from the point of view of administration but it is not a convenient arrangement for the people of Newfoundland. We have our own marine district and that should comprise the whole coastline of Newfoundland.
The minister also referred to a reclassification of lightkeepers' salaries and I am happy to hear him make that announcement. I would urge him to also look into the salaries of assistant lightkeepers and see what could be done about having the latter brought under the civil service commission in the same way as lightkeepers are. At the present time there is a vast inequity between the salaries paid to lightkeepers and their assistants. As I pointed out to the Minister of Labour when the committee was discussing his estimates, the latter are paid on the basis of prevailing rates. I brought this to the
Private Bills
attention of the Minister of Labour on August 16 and I would draw the attention of the Minister of Transport to what I said at that time. My remarks can be found at page 3867 of Hansard of that date. I do not wish to waste time repeating now what I said on that occasion.
However, I wish to remind the minister that the Department of Transport as well as the hydrographic service is a big sinner in this respect. I understand that the crews of the ships operated by his department at Halifax which do the same work and carry the same responsibility receive 11 per cent less pay than their counterparts in western parts of Quebec. In the interest of equity something should be done about this. As a national employer, I would suggest to the minister that a department of the federal government should follow the principle of equal pay for equal service regardless of where the service is performed. But if that is too wide a principle to adopt then I would point out there should certainly be no discrimination against people in the eastern provinces who do the same work and carry the same responsibility as people elsewhere and who should receive exactly the same pay. I urge the minister to consider the situation and correct these inequities.
Before taking my seat I should like to support the plea of the hon. member for St. John's East for an alternate airport. We all know that at the present time passenger and mail, freight and air cargo are held jup for weeks at a time when the existing airport is fogbound. An alternate airport should be constructed in a suitable locality ^is convenient to St. John's as Torbay. With the increasing volume of freight traffic ari alternate airport is necessary in any case.; This is looking into the future, too, but I do wish to support the remarks of the hop. member for St. John's East in that respect.
