speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something about this case. The bill has already been before the house on previous occasions and was recommitted to the private bills committee for the second time. There was no agreement on the bill in the committee and the division was very close.
This case gives an opportunity to members of parliament to scrutinize very closely what is wrong with the handling of divorces by parliament. In this instance there were five professional witnesses on the one side and on the other side the co-respondent who testified on his own behalf. Members of parliament are going to have to judge whether

the five professional witnesses told the truth or whether the co-respondent spoke the truth. On the one hand, the co-respondent said that he definitely could not have been in such and such a place on such and such a date and on the other hand these professional witnesses gave testimony that he was.
Therefore it behooves parliament to make a decision whether these people are going to be allowed to continue to come before parliament and perjure themselves or whether we are going to do something about it. I think we should take a look at just what happens in these cases. The Senate deals with divorce bills first before a committee where a decision is made. The House of Commons has the right, and has exercised it in contested cases on many occasions, to hear the evidence again or part of the evidence or additional evidence. The House of Commons is not an appeal court and does not function as such but exercises its right to examine such bills as it would any other private bill and to go into all the implications.
One of the problems that immediately confronts the House of Commons committee is that it has no power to subpoena witnesses. When a lawyer can come before members of a committee of the House of Commons and say that he will not bring forward such and such a witness, while at the same time we have no right to subpoena witnesses, I think it is very foolish to ask parliament to rule on such cases when parliament has no right to ask for all the evidence. If the committee of the House of Commons is going to be able to act properly then we must have the right that any court has in this type of case, and that certainly involves the fundamental right to subpoena witnesses in order to make sure that the whole story is heard. If the House of Commons is going to continue to operate a divorce mill and wishes to be honest, fair and just in its dealings with the people involved in these cases we are at least going to have to have that right.
There are many other handicaps under which we operate that have been highlighted by the Terry case. We find that the House of Commons can grant a divorce for any reason at all. Adultery does not have to be proved. It does not even have to be intimated that adultery took place. We can grant a divorce if we wish because the husband did not like the looks of his wife or the colour of her hair. The committee is completely within its rights in granting a divorce on such grounds.
On the other hand, apparently certain grounds are set out for the direction of the Senate in the granting of divorces. The Senate committees have been constituted in such a way that they can call witnesses.

Order. I think that I must ask the hon. member for Timiskaming to stick to the actual bill under consideration by the committee at this time. It appears to me that in his recent remarks he has been leaving the subject matter of the bill before the house. Would he kindly come back to the bill itself?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while my
remarks can be construed as being general they are also very pertinent to the Terry case because in that case the committee found that there were certain faults about which they had no power to do anything. The committee checked with the legal advisers of the House of Commons and found that it did not have the right to do the things to which I have referred.
Another factor that arose in this case has to do with the fact that when we hear evidence given on one side directly contradictory to evidence given by the other side we must have the right, which we did not have in this case, to investigate the circumstances surrounding that evidence. In this particular case the co-respondent testified that he assumed he had been in the Pembroke area. He assumed this because he had a gasoline statement indicating that on the day of the night in question he had purchased gasoline in Pembroke. I believe it was the evening of the tenth and the early hours of the morning of the eleventh that were in question. He established that it was his practice to go into an area such as Pembroke and spend two or three days there looking after his business. The man certainly is a very poor bookkeeper but I do not think that enters into the matter. He did have a receipt indicating that he was in the Pembroke area on the tenth and he did not say he did not have one that would indicate that he was there on the eleventh or twelfth.
The question boils down to the fact that his evidence is directly contradictory to the evidence given by the other witnesses in the case. They cannot all be right. Some of them must be wrong. Therefore I say that as a committee we are not functioning properly when we have not the right to send the R.C.M.P. to the Pembroke area to check the motels he may have stayed in-he also produced a motel receipt-and are not in a position to check the validity of his statements and the receipts which he produced. My experience is that when boards composed of laymen have been set up on a pseudo-legal basis they have checked immediately into receipts produced in evidence before them.
Private Bills-Divorce
When somebody has a signed statement, then that statement is immediately checked They have photostatic copies made anc checked for identification purposes. They have machinery set up that will allow them to function in a proper manner. If the exchequer court had been used to hear these divorce cases, as some hon. members of my party have suggested in the past, then that court would have been able to check into the evidence in a legal manner.
On the other hand, and I think this should be borne in mind, the evidence of private detectives is always in question when given in court. Defence counsel, Mr. McDonald, made a reference to this fact and backed it up with legal references which nobody questioned. I think, therefore, that statement will stand. It was pointed out in those references that these people are paid to do a certain job. We should take a look at the five men who were involved in this case under the direction of legal counsel. Some of them were on the job for nearly six months, and when you consider that these detectives receive $30 a day and expenses you can see that a great deal of money was put into this case. It would appear to me that the lawyer had told these men to either get the evidence or he would put somebody else on the job.
These men made certain statements which I believe should be checked by the R.C.M.P., especially when we consider that their evidence is always in question. A simple example of this was the matter of the driveway. On numerous occasions these detectives said the driveway would hold three automobiles. On the other hand, the defence said that it would hold only two automobiles, three if they were small English cars or if one were a small European sports car. This is a matter which could have been checked very easily. I feel this committee should have had the R.C.M.P. go there and measure the driveway to find out who was lying and who was not.
If we are going to accept evidence on face value, then why do we not recommend to legal counsel that they take their case to the Senate and let them hear the case? They do not care what happens over there, except when defence counsel gets up and says, we are going to contest this. Then, when the case comes to the House of Commons, defence counsel make their pitch. If this is the type of thing with which we are going to have to contend, then it is going to mean we would be well advised to tell the defence lawyer who is coming here to bring any theatrical witness he wants. He can make any statement he wants and can make as big a farce out of this committee as he wishes. Nothing will happen.

Private Bills-Divorce
We have not any right to commit these people for perjury. It has been said that we can ask the Ontario attorney general to investigate such a matter. According to my information it has happened once before, and the attorney general did exactly what I think he should have done. He said that he did not have time or it was not within his jurisdiction; he used some such method to by-pass it. He would have been very silly to bring a civil case from the province of Quebec into the Ontario courts and to have laid a perjury charge in connection with it.
Then we have the matter of the written evidence. We have here copies of the written evidence in these divorce cases in the Senate. This evidence was all taken down in the Senate, but when we heard this case we heard several witnesses that were not heard by the Senate. Now, the Senate has no desire to charge these people with perjury, and certainly they could not charge the people who did not give evidence before the Senate. We did not even have the evidence taken down because we were not constituted to do that. Would it not be a fine state of affairs if the private bills committee of the House of Commons were to go to the attorney general of Ontario and tell him that we would like to commit somebody for perjury on evidence which was not taken in a court of law and of which there is no transcript. I think it would be ridiculous to even suggest we would have the right to go to the Ontario court and ask for that type of charge.
These are some of the things that have plagued the House of Commons since it first started passing these divorce bills, and which have been highlighted in this Terry case. There are other things which have entered into this case. We have had a great deal of lobbying, and I understand that anyone who is going to lobby in the House of Commons must pay a fee and be registered as an official parliamentary agent. In many cases the people who have been doing the lobbying in this divorce case have been private citizens. I think we should have the right to prohibit these people from doing that type of lobbying. Other charges of intimidation have been made, and there are many other things that are better left unsaid, so I am not going to be put in the same category as the people who said them.
I think that we have in this bill probably all the fundamental problems that have faced the House of Commons since it started handling these divorce bills. I think it would not be out of order if I were to mention some of the things that could be done in the Terry case and in other cases to settle some of these problems. One of these things would

be the establishment of a committee at the next session to be charged with the responsibility of doing something about getting divorce out of the House of Commons. The committee could probably consider the bill that was introduced by a C.C.F. member on a number of occasions-

Order; I must take this opportunity to correct the speaker on something he said before, as well as the fact that he is off the bill again at the moment. He made a reference to the committee in the other place not caring about these particular cases, and I think that remark should be withdrawn. Any further remarks he makes on this bill should be confined to the bill itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
When I referred to the Senate not caring about this bill, I meant that the Senate had already ruled on it and expressed satisfaction with the evidence. When I said that the Senate did not care about it, I meant the Senate had finally disposed of this bill. The House of Commons is now considering it. I cannot speak for the Senate, but I doubt if they are going to review this bill. If they are, I would be very happy to have them do so. The chairman of our committee could suggest that the bill be withdrawn from our committee and be re-committed to the Senate. I do not think the remarks I made were out of order in that respect.
With all due respect, I would think that when we say something is wrong with this bill we should be given the right to say something constructive, and which would be advantageous to the procedure of this house. We should do something constructive towards moving these cases out of the House of Commons and into the exchequer court. If I am out of order in saying that, I will not say any more about it.
I think the committee has been faced with another problem, and that is when the committee makes a decision there is no fundamental right of appeal from that decision for the people affected.
If there were a court of law in the province, then they would have the right of appeal. We have had an appeal in the Terry case and we may have some more before this bill is finally satisfactory to a number of people. We may have appeals but they are strange appeals. They are just appeals where somebody recommits the bill to the committee after it has already been handled and a decision has been made. This may be an appeal, but in my opinion it does not satisfy the fundamental requirements or ensure the consideration that an appeal court presided over by a judge or judicial authority would give that type of appeal. The committee has

Private Bills-Divorce
not the right of sitting on appeal. Once the bill is passed, then there is no appeal from that decision as there would be if these cases were handled in any other manner.
I should like to make another suggestion, Mr. Chairman. We are all well aware of the reason why the Terry case and other cases go through the House of Commons. The reason this matter was not dealt with in the province of Quebec is to be found-and this is true of the province of Newfoundland -in their dislike of and their objection to divorce cases. That may well be and we do not want to discuss the grounds for that. But before the bills in many cases come into the House of Commons as private bills, there is litigation in the courts of Quebec for maintenance of children, for legal separation from the wife and in many of these cases- as in this one, I am quite sure-the adultery charge has been made. I would suggest that this may be another angle that the committee could investigate, namely that when the courts of Quebec rule-

Order. The hon. member has strayed away from the content of this bill on several occasions. I must ask him once and finally to confine his remarks to this bill or I shall be obliged [DOT] to ask him to take his seat.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am in agreement with the chairman of the committee who has said that we do not want to discuss personalities when we are discussing this bill. I am in agreement with him. I do not want to discuss personalities. I should like to make the statements general rather than refer to the persons concerned because I do not think such reference is fair. We are discussing this matter on a national basis and I do not think it is fair to the people concerned to discuss personalities. In many of these cases the defendant is going to be obliged to live in the community in which he or she is now living; and where children are involved, I do not like to see the children in the position of having had their names dragged through the mud, so to speak. But in cases where legal separation took place-and this is one of them-in my opinion it would have been much more advantageous if the courts in the province where the legal separation had taken place had proved or disproved the adultery charge at the same time they heard the rest of the case. Then we in the miscellaneous private bills committee would not be obliged to deal with this matter. The court would have already ruled on the legality of the adultery charge.
We are asked to make a decision on these adultery charges. The chairman would like me to refer to this case. This one is an
especially good one, if you wish to refer to personalities in this respect. The adultery charge itself in a few words is based on the following circumstances. On the night in question a number of people, five to be exact, came to the house; four of them came to the front door and one went to the back door. They tried to break down the front door. We smile at this. I think that that is something that any judge, if he were ruling on this case, would take exception to. They tried to break down the door. We are asked to condone this type of action. They tried to break down the door. They had no search warrant. They rapped on the door or rang the bell. There is a great deal of doubt in the evidence whether it is a bell, a buzzer or what it is. They make some kind of noise with a button anyway. Five minutes go by and the second time they make this noise with a button they hear footsteps. The man at the back hears footsteps. While they tried to knock down the front door, in the committee we find that the back door was open. All they had to do was to walk in. They did not need to break down the door. Then there were some footsteps coming down the stairs and five people ran around to the front door; there was a fight and there was a woman inside, and she got into the act and they had to fight her off. Then they were going up and down stairs and nobody knew whether they turned on the lights or not and the witnesses, in my opinion, were either very stupid or very smart. I consider that probably some of them are too smart for their own good, and if we could prove some of these perjury charges against them, maybe that would cool them off.
Anyway, no one seems to know whether the lights were on or off, and nobody tells the same story. They picked up clothes and they searched all through these rooms; they searched through the clothes closets in the two bedrooms, and all this takes place in only two and a half minutes. In that time they visited all the clothes closets and they found lipstick on the pillow cases. The two pillows had been mussed up and then they went downstairs and gave a cursory glance around the place. Then they went down to the basement and it was dark, but they found someone in the basement, and he had his shirt open.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Frankly, I do not care if hon. members like it or not, this is what happened as I heard it in the committee.

You know what happened; everyone knows what happened.

I do not want to talk about it, but we are in committee. We go down -they go down the stairs-
We go down?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have been taken up and down those stairs so many times in this particular case that if I say "we" it is because of that fact. Next we are in a bedroom which is normally occupied by the owner's son, and we have a great deal of difficulty in finding out what kind of a bed is there; whether this 36-inch bed was a camp cot or whether it is a single bed or three-quarter bed, but in any event we are in the bedroom which has been fixed up and probably sound-proofed to a certain extent, and there is a man there who said he has taken a couple of aspirin and had been lying down to relieve himself of a headache.
In any event, these two people, the respondent and the co-respondent were supposed to have been together, but the committee members will recall that the nearest we could establish these two people had been found together was when they were in an automobile and that when they were in the house itself the nearest they were ever proved to be to each other was when one was in the basement and the other was in an upstairs bedroom. This is the evidence which was produced in the committee by five professional witnesses, which is supposed to prove adultery.
What about a little bit of order?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On the other hand, I certainly did not appreciate the type of evidence given by the co-respondent, which was flamboyant and in many cases he ran away with the cross-examining lawyer. His evidence was not substantiated in many respects, it was contradictory, although it was given under oath. In some instances he was supposed to have been in the Quebec area for two or three days and in other cases in Pembroke, while the detectives had said he was somewhere else. All this evidence should have been checked by the committee and I also believe that the evidence respecting the car in question should have been checked. There was a great deal of talk about the kind of automobile which was supposed to have been taken from here to there and there to here, back and forth on different nights.
I think that if we had had the proper facilities at our disposal we could have examined the situation respecting this witness and could have found out whether or not he was telling the truth. I am quite sure that the counsel representing both the defendant and respondent in this case would

have been most happy if the committee had been able to decide which side was telling the truth, because we were faced with a problem as to which of the witnesses had lied. We knew these things were contradictory and we had to assume that these people were perjuring themselves. I think we are not being unfair in assuming that this committee next year may well have to hear this case again so that it should be able to call witnesses. If the committee exists as it does today-and I hope it does not-it should have the power to cite the people who are giving false testimony and it should have the power to do something about it when such people are cited.
The committee should also have at its disposal the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in order to investigate such matters as the committee itself decides should be investigated. If the lawyers are not in a position to prove or disprove, or do not make any attempt to prove or disprove evidence considered to be pertinent to the case, then the committee must have this right, and there must be the right to appeal.
There have been other cases, including the Gregory case, in respect of which the committee has leaned over backwards-
Order. * The hon. member's time has expired.

The hon. member has stated that five professional witnesses in this case have committed perjury respecting adultery, and yet at the end of his statement he also told the committee that he did not know whether or not the co-respondent was telling the truth.
The fact of the matter is that either the five witnesses are not telling the truth, and are therefore committing perjury, or the two witnesses, the wife and the co-respondent, are not telling the truth and they are therefore committing perjury.
This matter was thrashed out with the help of a great deal of evidence for over a day and a half and, as the hon. member has pointed out, there was a good deal of argument in the committee about the conflicting evidence and the eventual decision of the committee was very, very close. I do not intend to give my own views this afternoon but rather to draw to the attention of this committee as briefly as I can the evidence, both pro and con, so that the committee in its own time can make its decision in this matter.
Firstly, the hon. member stated that there was lipstick on the pillow of Mrs. Terry. On reading the evidence and checking my notes I do not believe any such evidence was presented. If it had been so presented that would be a very telling point against her

but, in fairness to the respondent in this case, I do not believe there was any such evidence.
The hon. member has mentioned the conflicting evidence of the five professional witnesses-a mixed bag of detectives-and in that regard he is perfectly correct. There was firstly the question of the door bell, as to whether it was a door bell with a regular ring or a gong; secondly, the position of the stairway in the house, which was of some importance, and whether the stairway had treads; thirdly, there was the question of the light in the basement; and, fourthly, whether footsteps were heard pounding downstairs from the bedroom; there was conflicting evidence on all those points.
On the other hand, we have the allegations of the petitioner that on five different occasions the co-respondent was found in the home of the respondent. According to the two detectives, they took up surveillance there on the night of May 21, when the two parties, the respondent and the co-respondent, were in the house. The detectives remained until 1.20 the following morning, when the Pointe Claire police came along and cleared them out of the area. On July 10 two of the detectives took up surveillance and the two parties were inside the house when the detectives left at 3.30 the following morning. At least, if the co-respondent had left the home before that time they had not seen him leave.
The two detectives kept up surveillance during the night of July 31 and when the detectives left at 8.00 a.m. on August 1 they had not seen the co-respondent leave. On August 13 they again kept surveillance and on this occasion the two professional witnesses saw the co-respondent leave the home of the wife at 7.40 the next morning. Then we come down to the date of August 30, which is the date about which most of the evidence was presented, and my friend has already given the committee a very good synopsis of the evidence concerning that particular evening.
These were the problems facing the committee. We heard these professional witnesses give conflicting evidence on the points I have mentioned and there was conflicting evidence, perhaps, on other points as well. Perhaps one might expect this to be the case or, on the other hand, if they all told the same story we could very well say they told a patched up story. It is a very difficult problem, as the closeness of the committee's decision would indicate. One could not really tell who was telling the truth and who was telling a lie. I do not think anyone in his heart of hearts could have said definitely "That fellow is telling the truth and that fellow is telling a
Private Bills-Divorce
lie." You have to draw your suppositions or inferences from the evidence as to who seems to be presenting the better case and whose story seems to hold water.
In that connection may I quote two remarks made by the co-respondent under cross-examination. First, when he was asked about kissing Mrs. Terry he said, in answer to the question, "Did you kiss Mrs. Terry?" "Not to my knowledge." Secondly, he was asked a question arising out of the detectives' evidence that on August 31 he was seen bare-waisted in the lady's bedroom. The question was asked after a great deal of conflicting testimony as to whether the nearby street was 50 feet, 75 feet, 125 feet, 150 feet, 300 feet or 500 feet away from this particular bedroom window, and was as follows: "Were you ever bare to the waist in the woman's bedroom?" And his answer was, "I don't think I was ever in that bedroom stripped to the waist. Also I don't think you could see into that bedroom from the street."
This was the difficulty we had with the witnesses, and it is unfair to quote just two examples of their evidence and to say that they are not to be believed because of the type of evidence they gave. My hon. friend will probably agree that we also had a good deal of trouble with the co-respondent. He tended to be too rapid with his answers and time after time for his own protection I had to try to slow him down and to tell him to think about his answers, not to try to rationalize them but not to blurt out something for which he would be sorry.
There was evidence one way and the other, and I might say that from the wife's standpoint and that of the co-respondent they both appeared before us and denied under oath that they had had sexual intercourse. When you have such a denial under oath you have to pay very great attention to it, and you cannot dismiss it lightly. As the hon. member who has just spoken remarked, we had suggestions from the respondent's lawyer, Mr. John McDonald of Ottawa, who is a very experienced counsel, that we must be very careful in the way in which we look at the evidence of professional detectives. He quoted from an old English case, and also from a more recent one, Sopwith versus Sop-with, and that is perfectly proper. That is the law and we have those directions to guide us. We were also very fortunate in having Dr. Maurice Ollivier, the law clerk in constant attendance upon our committee, and he was available for questions about the probability of certain matters with respect to inferential law, which was an important guide to the members of the committee before making up their minds. After a couple

Private Bills-Divorce
of days of hearings under our belts we finally made our decision and reported it to the House of Commons.

Mr. Chairman, as this is probably the last occasion when divorce cases will be discussed during this session I should like to say a few words on this case.
I have been a member of the committee on miscellaneous private bills for a great many years. As one hon. member has pointed out, this was a most difficult case-one of the most difficult cases I can ever remember-and one which illustrates the difficulties under which the committee labours in discharging its duties. This is certainly one committee from which I would be most happy to be excused, but I serve on it because I accept it as part of my parliamentary duties. This committee has responsibility to this house because it is set up by this house, and it also has a responsibility to the parties who appear before it and who will be affected by its decisions. In cases such as this it also has another responsibility, namely to see that our traditions of justice are maintained. The history of this case shows very clearly as the hon. member for Timiskaming pointed out, that the miscellaneous private bills committee cannot possibly discharge its responsibilities as it is presently set up.
If we go back through the history of this case we find it came before the Senate divorce committee and then it came before the miscellaneous private bills committee. In that committee we heard arguments from lawyers on behalf of each Of the parties. On the basis of those arguments we decided not to grant this divorce. I may say here that our responsibilities to this house are greatly increased by the fact that there is no written record. Every member of this committee will have to say yea or nay and vote on this bill depending largely upon what we tell the committee in order to form an honest opinion. Having heard this case for the first time and having rejected this application for divorce the bill came before you and was recommitted to the committee in order that further evidence might be heard.
On the first occasion we heard only the arguments of the lawyers for each of the parties but this time we called witnesses. Here, again, we have to depend on our memories, for there is no written record of what was actually said. One of these witnesses was on his feet for nearly two hours being grilled by a lawyer and while I did not regard him as a very good witness and while there was lots about him I did not like I must say that if I were in his place and on trial there being grilled for two hours I am afraid I would get tripped up with regard to some of the things I might say.
[Mr. McCleave.l
Having heard the evidence and having had an opportunity to size up the witnesses personally and to arrive at a better judgment, because we had the opportunity to judge not only the words that were said but the people who said them, we made another decision and recommended that a divorce be granted. That points up one of the weaknesses of the miscellaneous private bills committee in that we do not have any fixed set of rules or procedures. Here is a decision which affects people's lives-the most serious decision that this house can make because it affects the lives of these people and the people connected with them, their relatives and so on 

and yet that decision was made on the basis of a simple majority. Members know that attendance at a committee of that kind is never 100 per cent perfect; there is always someone missing, and I get the horrible feeling inside me that if those who happen to be absent were there in the committee and if somebody else was absent the decision would be different, and one of the things which I think this house must consider in cases such as this is that decisions should be based not on a simple majority but on a two-thirds majority-certainly not on a simple majority, at least-to offset the factor of people coming in late, of people who attend only part of the hearing and so on, and to offset also the factors that work inside ourselves, because when we hear evidence we like to be objective-we like to set ourselves apart altogether and be totally impartial, but because we are human beings we cannot do that. There is in each one of us a propensity, I suppose, to believe the worst of anyone and this is very hard to get out of your mind, and it is hard to be absolutely impartial when you are hearing evidence.
There is in everyone of us a tendency, also, to react against other individuals. A certain witness will say something, and say it in a way which will sort of rile you; you react against it, and that is something we cannot help. And there is in most of us, I suppose, a propensity to sympathize with the underdog. These are all factors which interfere with the balance of our judgment. There must be factors in this committee to offset all the other factors which are likely to offset our judgment in matters like this. We are all sincerely endeavouring to do our best and do what we believe is right but we have a haunting fear that whatever we do we have a 50 per cent chance of being wrong.
There was only one witness in this case who, I believe, did not tell one lie, and that was the son of Mrs. Terry, a young boy of 17 or 18 years of age. He was straightforward and very convincing. In the evidence of all

the other witnesses there were flaws and it is not right to pick out one and say one was more reliable than another. There are flaws in all their evidence. However, when we come to make our decisions we have a responsibility to uphold the tradition of justice on which we have prided ourselves down through the centuries and that tradition is that a person is innocent unless proved guilty. We must be certain, the proof must be convincing and it must relate to certain days specified.
There is any amount of suspicion in cases like this, but suspicion is not enough. You cannot judge a case on suspicion. There must be proof, and opportunity is not enough. As the chairman pointed out this afternoon there were five occasions when the respondent and the co-respondent were together in the house. There was opportunity, but there was no proof, and on four of those occasions there was no proof that they were alone in this house. There could have been other people present, children or visitors. All we know is that these people were alone in the house at the time the detectives broke in but they were found in separate parts of the house and we do not know who was present prior to the break-in. You cannot say that proof of adultery lies in the fact that two people are alone in a house. Reference was made to the fact that the gentleman was bare to the waist but even if that were true it is no proof of adultery because the woman might not have been in the room with him at any time. The argument was pinned on those circumstances on the night the detectives broke in to secure the evidence.
The very fact that people in their desire to secure evidence of adultery will go to the length of violating the law and breaking down a person's door and invading their privacy causes me to place little reliance on whatever evidence they give. I am suspicious because they were prepared to go to such lengths to secure the evidence.
We also must consider what will be the results of granting this divorce. If I vote for or against it I have a 50-50 chance of being wrong because it is almost impossible to reach an accurate decision on the basis of the evidence presented in this case. Also I must as an individual consider what will be the results of my voting for this bill and I must attempt to take the course of action that will produce the least harmful results. If I were to vote in favour of the preamble of this bill carrying I must consider some of the following results. In the first place if the committee votes for the bill it will have taken a step that cannot be retraced. Once the divorce is granted the marriage is
Private Bills-Divorce
terminated. If we do that we are in effect reversing the tradition of British law by saying that because a person is suspected of misconduct he is guilty and he has to prove his innocence and that because he has not proved his innocence he is guilty. But we have no positive proof of actual adultery. This couple were found in the same house but in different parts of it when the detectives broke in. Although the detectives had been following these people for a number of months they had witnessed no open display of affection between them.
All hon. members know that a great deal of the evidence that comes before us in these cases is evidence that is contrived, set up or manufactured. People arrange to be found together in compromising circumstances but in every other case of which I have knowledge at least the two parties concerned were found in the same room and there was supporting evidence in that a bed was ruffled or there was underwear strewn about or some other supporting evidence. If because two people are found in the same building, one in the attic and one in the basement, they are guilty of adultery, we are establishing an extremely bad precedent and making it easier in future for people who want divorces to manufacture evidence.
On the other hand, however, hon. gentlemen must consider that if we do not pass the bill the situation will remain as is and the marriage will not be dissolved. If the wife has been guilty of misconduct she will no doubt persist in it and there will be another opportunity provided for her husband to secure more substantial evidence to place before us. For the above reasons I cannot support the carrying of this preamble.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Halifax who serves very capably as chairman of the committee on miscellaneous and private bills highlighted one of the most important features of the work of the committee when he referred to the difficulty of the committee particularly in cases of this nature to reach an honest and sound decision. I have been bothered a great deal by the fact that difficult cases of this nature are rendered even more difficult when hon. members of the committee are as rushed as we have been during this session. I speak from personal experience, one which I am sure is shared by most hon. members serving on that committee, when I say I find great difficulty in concentrating on these cases because other thoughts keep going through my mind. One thinks of a speech one must prepare for a certain time, one wonders if a certain report is yet available and one remembers a couple of letters one should have answered the day before but overlooked. I submit that

Supply-Transport
hon. members are in no position to reach sound decisions with respect to difficult cases when they are as busy as we have been this session.
The history of this case has been outlined by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. The case came before the committee of the other place, was passed by the other place, reached the house, was rejected and referred back to the committee. When it concluded its discussions the committee was split down the middle. One side was as convinced they were right as they were that the other side was wrong.
An important fact to bear in mind is that if we pass this bill we are establishing an extremely bad precedent.
Six o'clock.
We can all see what this will inevitably lead to in the future.
Order. It being six o'clock, shall I rise, report progress and request leave to consider this bill again at the next sitting of the house?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

Mr. Chairman,
although I almost committed myself to the minister that I would not participate in this debate I hope he will forgive me for taking a few minutes of the time of the committee to say a few words in French on this item.
(Translation):
First, I would like to say what a happy choice it was when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) appointed Mr. Hees as Minister of Transport. It is true that it is not too easy to follow in the footsteps of men like the member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and Mr. George Marler; but I must say that the present Minister of Transport knows his job, 
and that you will never find a more affable person. But knowing how very modest he is, I suppose he would not take issue with me when I say that even the passage of time will not give him the profound knowledge possessed by his predecessors.
On that note, I wish him the best of good luck-and that does not mean I hope he has to spend too long burdened with the administration of the Department of Transport.
I shall conclude these opening remarks by saying that he can consider it an honour to be appointed Minister of Transport. My personal experience has very often given me first-hand insight into the high standard of efficiency and the conscientiousness of senior officials and personnel in the Department of Transport. I am revolted at the childish and baseless charges made in the press by the one whom I must still call the "honourable" member for Brantford (Mr. Wratten).
Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the minister and congratulate him for his speech when he introduced his estimates. Considering the short time he has been in office, I think he has shown that he has really "gone to it" and that while he has perhaps not solved all the problems of Canadians in this field, he has grasped them. May I also pay tribute to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who held the portfolio of transport for 9 years and who personally announced the construction of the Beattyville-Chibouga-mau railroad.
By the skin of his teeth.

Oh, "by the skin of his teeth"! May I ask why? Of course, the jab comes from a government member; there are a few of them who like interjecting, which is just about all they're able to contribute to the debates of the house. Just the same I will-
Come to the point, assuming you have a point.

If the member for Lake St. John (Mr. Parizeau) wanted to get up and say something perhaps we could reply to him-even regarding the Lake St. John airport in Alma.
I thank the former administration for having given us the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railway. Many things were said during the last elections, and even during the 1957 campaign, about the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railroad. I have no doubt that several members in the opposition, even my predecessor

and Mr. Gagnon, the hon. member for Chicoutimi, have made inquiries in this house and took some steps in order to intercede with the minister. I do not deny that they made some effort, but I also want to commend Mr. Andre Gauthier, the distinguished predecessor of the hon. member for Lake St. John and also the former hon. member for Roberval, Mr. Georges Villeneuve, who urged my former employer, the Hon. George Marler, to proceed with the project. And I am all the better in a position to know what I am talking about because at that time I was Mr. Marler's humble secretary, and Messrs. Gauthier and Villeneuve pressed Mr. Marler so much that at one time the former minister of transport told me: "Now, you'll just have to tell them to stop bothering me; I know we must build a railway between St. Felicien and Chibougamau, and we are going to build it."
If I say this, Mr. Chairman, it is because many electors of the constituencies of Lake St. John, Lapointe, Chicoutimi and Roberval have heard another story. I do not in the least intend to minimize the merit of all those who spoke in favour of the railway between Chibougamau and St. Felicien. Mr. Gagnon spoke about it; my predecessor in the constituency of Lapointe, Mr. Girard, spoke about it, but the fact remains that the Liberal government gave us the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railway.
During the last election campaign and even during the campaign of 1957, I heard a candidate state that it was through the intervention of members of the opposition that the construction of the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railroad had been decided. No doubt the committee will allow me to recall a witty remark made over television by a former Liberal member who said: "If you are willing to give credit to the Quebec Liberal opposition for the Talbot boulevard in our area, we are ready, on our part, to give credit to the Conservative opposition for the construction of the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railroad".
In that connection, Mr. Chairman, I also wish to pay tribute to Mr. Grenier, the late lamented secretary of the Conseil economique de I'orientation du Saguenay. Before he died, over a year ago, he had made great efforts and had pleaded on several occasions with Mr. Marler for the construction of the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railway.
The Minister of Transport will perhaps allow me, and I believe this is about all I
Supply-Transport
am going to say on the first item because I do not want to take up all the time of the committee, to read a letter that was sent to me by the president of the brotherhood of railroad employees of my riding, about the lay-offs which have been made in that organization, respecting the number of miles for the section men in the Lake St. John-Saguenay areas.
Mr. Chairman, I beg your pardon, but I will only read a short part of this letter into the record. I hope that the minister will avail himself of the good offices of his deputy, who speaks French very well, or of those of the marine services where there are quite a number of people quite conversant in that language. As a matter of fact the minister himself speaks French very well indeed. I would like, then, to read a passage from a letter I have received from the chairman of the railway employees union of my area:
At the regular quarterly meeting of the Brotherhood Maintenance of Way Employees' local 417, held at Jonquiere on April 5 last, it was proposed and unanimously carried that a letter should be sent to you to congratulate you on your election-
In this instance I am not alone. There are three other members from the area who were elected along with me. I continue:
-and to wish you a long life in the service of Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that I will have a long life in the service of Canadians.
I have also been asked to acquaint you with the facts and to ask your help to stop a project which high officials of the C.N.R. have been considering for a fairly long time, a decision which would not be very beneficial to our area since it would tend to lower the standards of security and speed, and to curtail the service and improvements on the ''Laurentian" division. Under this project, the sections which now are 7 to 8 miles long and are manned by three sectionmen would be increased to 12 to 15 miles for about the same number of men, thus causing the dismissal of 50 or 60 regular workers out of a total number of 300 who look after 600 miles of railroad.
As you are not acquainted with the work of regular sectionmen who look after the maintenance and upkeep of the railway line, I may tell you that a section crew is made up of a foreman and two men who have from 7 to 8 miles to maintain, which means that they have to patrol the area, inspect the rails, change them when necessary, change the sleepers, mend the fences, level the line, keep it straight, take care of public and farm crossings, of ditches, sideways, switches, in short maintain everything belonging to the C.N.R.
Moreover, our winters with snow, ice and frost considerably increase the amount of work to be done.
I shall add that the dieselization did not reduce our task so that, as in other departments, this changeover to another form of power cannot be invoked as a reason for decreasing the number of regular employees. Mr. Gordon once said that sectionmen were the backbone of the railways.

Supply-Transport
Consequently, their number cannot be reduced without endangering the security of the passengers, the employees and the equipment. People may say that in other divisions such a rearrangement of sections actually did take place, but I can assure you that ours is not comparable to any other.
I perfectly understand the attitude of the C.N.R. management in this respect. I do not want to criticize Mr. Gordon, because I have seen too many hon. members in the opposition, including the present hon. Minister of Transport, putting the blame on the National Railways authorities. I had the pleasure of working with several C.N.R. officials and I know-and to my mind the hon. Minister of Transport knows it too-that Mr. Gordon and his colleagues are doing a tremendous job for the Canadian National Railways. They do so in a spirit of devotion and competence, which is second to none among the employees to that of other crown corporations in our country.
I am not questioning the decision of the authorities. I merely note the fact that from 30 to 40 employees were laid off on account of that decision. I shall certainly not criticize the president of the Canadian National Railways for trying to administer the company intelligently and on a business-like basis. He is a very competent man and, I repeat, he is second to none in the country as far as competence is concerned in the exercise of his duties. However, the government will perhaps admit that there is a problem there, because among those who are laid off, there are married people with families to bring up, and who have worked 10, 12, or 15 years for the Canadian National Railways. They learned a trade that they cannot exercise in private industry, elsewhere than in the Canadian National Railways or in the Canadian Pacific Railways. That is a grim situation. I also ask the hon. minister, when the session is over, to have my speech read to one of his officials and to communicate with the C.N.R. authorities to see if there is no way of overcoming this thorny problem.
At the beginning of my remarks, I said I would not take up too much of the committee's time. I will just say this: I know the member for Saguenay (Mr. LaRue) complained this afternoon about the former Liberal administration not having done much for his constituency. Of course, he was careful not to refer to what they actually did; he simply concentrated on what they had not done in his riding. I do not reproach him for trying to help his riding, but regarding the former Liberal administration, he could have been a little more objective and could have tried to grant some credit.

I call upon the hon. minister to be good enough to have my speech read by one of his officials, so that he can tackle this problem; I thank him in advance for his kind attention.
(Text):

You are about to see an example, Mr. Chairman, of the benefit of an extended discussion. I came into the house last evening prepared to speak for at least 40 minutes. This morning, I changed my mind and cut that down by 50 per cent. This afternoon, as the discussion wore on, I threw away my speech. Tonight, I am only going to detain the committee for a short time to discuss one matter that is of real importance in my district and that is the problem that arises from the conflict of interests between navigation and the lumber interests in our district. It is a matter that is the result of what I might call the lack of teeth in the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
I am going to outline the problem as briefly as I can, then I should like to say what has been done about it and what I think should be done about it. It is a problem that can be fully corrected only by action of this parliament. It is brought about by what I might call the misuse of the Sturgeon river by certain companies, and in this case I have in mind one company, in the movement of logs down that river. The river is very important to the people of my district. There is the tourist industry, which is tremendously important; there are other activities across the lake and there are the local people who like to enjoy the facilities that the river provides. All of these people are handicapped by what I call the misuse of this river in these logging operations.
In the past when the drive was on in the spring the logs were shot down the river with complete disregard for the people who normally use those waters. The matter usually came to the attention of the council or chamber of commerce, and they in turn perhaps discussed the matter together and then went to the offending firm. Sometimes results were obtained. In later years, the matter generally came to the member of parliament. I know this process has been going on for the last 30 years. The member then would appeal to the minister. Until three or four years ago the member usually went to the minister of public works and members of the engineering branch, most of whom worked at that time out of Ottawa, used to visit the area. All of this takes time,

and by the time the engineering branch visited the area, nature or the offending company had usually corrected the problem. However, there was no permanent solution.
Time went along, and in 1955 we were able to get the two companies that now use the river together with the Sturgeon Falls council and the members of the chamber of commerce. At that meeting there was a recognition of the problem and a promise that this misuse would not be committed in the future. Since that time the one company has been most co-operative and has avoided moving logs on holiday week-ends or when there was insufficient water in the river. They have had a regard for the interests of other people using these waters. The other company, it seems, still continues to disregard their responsibilities in this area.
As recently as a few days ago I received another telegram which I should like to take the time to read to the committee. This is a telegram from the Sturgeon Falls chamber of commerce and is directed to me. It reads: Contractor for J. B. Smith Company started moving logs through sluice about ten days ago. Loose logs in Minniha-Sa bay and Sturgeon river makes navigation most dangerous. Conditions last weekend were the worst in past ten years. Tourists trying to go across the lake had to detour to Lavigne. It is evident that the contractor is deliberately disregarding safety of those travelling on the river. Several thousand logs were released last week-end even when it was apparent that waters above dam would not be released because of shortage. Please pray the Minister of Transport to see that conditions are remedied as soon as possible. Gordon Lumber Co. gave us full co-operation this year.
Mr. Chairman, I have stated the matter. I have brought it to the attention of the minister personally, and I know he is giving it his attention. Part I of the Navigable Waters Protection Act has to do with permits for construction of things in and on navigable waters. Part II of the Navigable Waters Protection Act deals with the use to which these waters can be put. I raised this matter when the Navigable Waters Protection Act was amended in 1956. At that time I thought perhaps an amendment could be made to part I. However, upon reflection, I think this legislation can only be amended as to part II. There could be a solution to this problem if teeth were put into this legislation. In the past, when officials of the department have gone to the area it would depend perhaps on how hard they stamped their feet whether or not they obtained desirable results. However, if teeth are put into this legislation this problem can be solved. I should like to suggest an interdepartmental committee. I had this suggestion close to realization at one time. I am now suggesting it again. I suggest that perhaps an interdepartmental
Supp ly-Transport
committee could be set up of representatives of the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport to study this problem with a view to bringing in an amendment to the Navigable Waters Protection Act that would specifically spell out this problem and the corrective.
Before I take my seat I should like to thank the Minister of Transport for the kind and sympathetic attention he gave to a request earlier this year in connection with the relocating of the administration or terminal building at the North Bay airport. I would not want this opportunity to pass without thanking the minister on my own behalf and particularly on behalf of the chamber of commerce and the other people in my district who are so greatly interested. I wonder whether the minister has anything further to say as to the progress on that project.

I might just answer the hon. member now on that matter. I should like to assure him first of all that we are looking into the question that he first raised. I can tell him that we shall do our very best to work out the best possible solution for that very real problem which the people he has mentioned are running into.
Second, with regard to North Bay airport terminal building, I am glad to be able to report that a new civil area for development of civil terminal facilities has been selected quite separate from the military installations. Engineering planning is proceeding now and we hope that we may be able to commence some clearing during the winter this year and that with further development the construction contract can be let next year.

Mr. Chairman, I will not take up too much time of the committee at this stage. I am going to take a cue from the minister in past years. He always said what he had to say in about ten minutes. It has always been my considered opinion that it should not take a person 30 minutes to build up what he had to, say in ten minutes.
At this time, Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the minister for his kindness in the grant that he has given us in Leeds county and the city of Brockville for the municipal airport. I should like to bring to the attention of the committee something about which I have spoken frequently in past years, namely the condition of the railway station which we have had to put up with now for a good number of years. This station in Brockville is outdated and outmoded and if it stands much longer it will be outlawed. It was built shortly after the Grand Trunk railway was completed between Montreal and Toronto. I feel that it was built to accommodate the

Supply-Transport
people of Brockville at a time when Brock-ville was a very small town. But I might say the population of Brockville has increased about 100 per cent in the past 18 years. It is now a thriving city. I believe that the people of Brockville are deserving of a station in proportion to the prospects for the future and that the industry which is thriving there at the present time merits nothing less. The city of Brockville is on the eastern outskirts of the Thousand islands and is indeed in what I might call Leeds the lovely.
I have another problem which I wish to bring before the committee this evening, namely the level crossing on William street in Brockville. It is extremely inconvenient. Not only that, but it is dangerous. Brockville is expanding to the north. That is the only way it has to expand. William street, which crosses the double tracks of the C.N.R. from Montreal to Toronto and also the main C.P.R. line from Brockville to Ottawa, is closed off by the several trains that pass over those tracks during the 24 hours of the day. It is a serious matter. We have schools in this vicinity and another large school is being built at the present time north of those tracks which children are obliged to cross. Not only that, but these tracks are closed off by passing trains and trains which are stationary at the station, sometimes for intervals of quite some duration.
I should like to give a good illustration of that situation. Not too long ago an ambulance was hurrying a patient to the hospital-a catastrophe patient-and it did not get there in time for medical aid. Not only that, but it has been known in the not too distant past that a maternity ambulance had to stop at this crossing and I might say that the results were rather regrettable. There are three highways passing over this street, namely highways 29, 42 and the road from the new highway 401, which bypasses Brockville. Increased traffic to Brockville will come over that route. Within another year traffic will be terrific and I say without hesitation that it is time that something is done with regard to this level crossing in order to make it less hazardous and more convenient for the people.
I have spoken on this matter on several occasions in this house but apparently what I have said has fallen on deaf ears. I am happy to state now that negotiations are under way at the present time between the three levels of government, namely the board of transport commissioners, the provincial department of highways and the municipal government of the city of Brockville. I am hopeful that no stone will be left unturned in an effort to bring about immediate improvements and that a subway or overpass may be

constructed on this street which will make passage more convenient and less hazardous. I hope the minister will use his influence in every way he can to eliminate this obstacle and to further the building of this subway which will be much appreciated by the residents of the area which I have the honour to represent.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to present to the new Minister of Transport a problem which I hope in the months ahead, when the pressure of work will not be so urgently upon him, he will very seriously consider and which I hope he will bring to the attention of his colleagues in the cabinet and to the attention of interested parties in the lower mainland of British Columbia in order to see whether or not a new approach can be instituted. I have in mind the problem of the Fraser river. We now have a new government and a new minister and I am hoping that he can restore a bit of order out of the mess of confusion which exists in the mouth of that river.
As the minister knows, we have in New Westminster what is known as the New Westminster harbour board; in south Burnaby we have the north Fraser harbour board, and we also have the national harbours board administering most of the other waters in and around the mouth of the Fraser river. Large areas of water and shoreline are really nobody's business at all, although technically speaking all of what used to be the wilderness areas of the waterfront were at one time assigned to the national harbours board and therefore come under the jurisdiction of the harbour master in Vancouver. Actually these areas have received no attention from the government, from the harbour master or from any of the harbour boards for a very long period of years, and with the upset of the government many of the municipalities concerned are very, very optimistic for the future and they are now hoping that out of the tens of millions of dollars voted annually for the purpose of looking after the mouth of the Fraser river a little bit of development will come their way.
There are many conflicting interests involved in the administration of the waters of the Fraser river and I believe it is not by evil design but that it is primarily because of these conflicting interests that many matters have not received attention which should have received attention and that very large sums of money now being voted each year are an absolute waste. The federal government has a number of ministers who are involved. When it comes to taking the water off the land, the Minister of Agriculture is

concerned; when it comes to making surveys the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is concerned, and he has a large vote with respect to the Fraser river in his estimates; when it comes to taking sand out to enable ships to navigate and to building the breakwaters the Minister of Public Works is concerned. The Minister of Transport is concerned with the harbours in the area and the Minister of Agriculture is concerned with the problem of erosion of the rich agricultural land. The Minister of Fisheries is very much concerned with what happens in and around the mouth of the Fraser river and in an emergency, such as that which happened a few years ago in British Columbia, the whole cabinet is involved. On that occasion, in 1948, it had to vote many, many millions of dollars to augment the even greater number of dollars spent by the British Columbia government to alleviate the conditions caused by the flooding of the river. The Minister of Public Works is also involved with respect to this river when it comes to the building of bridges across it.
Our British Columbia government also has many ministers involved in what happens on the Fraser river. The minister in charge of highways has to look after the bridges, and the minister of fisheries in British Columbia is concerned. Another minister deals with the building of dikes along the river banks. The British Columbia government is vitally concerned that the river should be adequately used by the lumber interests and we have in the heart of my riding the largest sawmill in the British commonwealth, which is situated on the banks of the Fraser river. The government of British Columbia is also concerned that this river may be an important source for the development of hydroelectric energy. There are others who are concerned, it will be seen, besides the Minister of Transport. There are the farmers, the fishermen, the shipping interests, the longshoremen, the industrial concerns and those who are interested in the recreational possibilities of the shorelines of the lower mainland.
I remember the Minister of Public Works, when he was in the opposition, for some time advocating to the then minister of transport that that minister should accept the establishment of an advisory committee to the national harbours board and I believe that what the Minister of Public Works had in mind was that on this advisory committee might be found representatives of the various, and at times, conflicting, interests. The then minister of transport, after hours of coaxing, eventually agreed that there was merit in the
Supp ly-Transport
suggestion of an advisory committee composed of local interests who were concerned with the matter, somewhat similar to that which existed in respect of the harbour board at Halifax. I understand, however, that such a committee has never been established; it was left more or less in the hands of one of the aldermen of the city of Vancouver, who apparently did very little about it.
I wish the minister would look into that possibility, particularly to see if an advisory committee established to assist the national harbours board in the administration of harbour facilities in the lower mainland could have on it adequate representation from the municipal corporations affected. I would like to go much further and to see established a Fraser river board or a Fraser river authority, having a board composed of representatives of all municipalities from the mouth of the Fraser all the way up to Hope. The federal and provincial governments might then reach an agreement whereby they could through their various authorities supply the technical and administrative personnel necessary. However, this Fraser river authority, constituted of all the interests concerned, would lay down the general policy as to how, when and where things were to be done along this vital river.
This river is of vital importance to most of the people of our province. On this Fraser river board should be, primarily, representatives of municipal bodies, of the shipping companies, of industrial interests-in particular, lumber and fisheries-of labour-the longshoremen's and fishermen's unions and the agriculture organizations.
What kind of work would this Fraser river board do? First of all it would do the work now being done by the national harbours board, the New Westminster board and the North Fraser harbour board. This board would replace these local boards and would undertake a much more comprehensive organization, an organization which would be much wider in its interests than the interests being served at the present time.
The first responsibility of a Fraser river board would be to undertake a complete survey of the potentialities of the river. This has been recommended to the Minister of Public Works and, I believe, to the Minister of Transport by the lower mainland regional planning board. This is an organization which has very excellent advisers. They have technical men on their payroll and they have received the active support of the municipal corporations along the banks of the Fraser, bodies from which they derive most of their income.

Supply-Transport
This lower mainland planning board has asked that the potentialities of this river be explored. We cannot have proper and economic development of this river unless a survey is made of all its potentialities. This would avoid much of the overlapping which now takes place. It would ensure that shipping interests would not be hampered from time to time by the lack of an adequate dredging program. For several weeks in almost each and every year ocean-going vessels cannot load grain because the federal government has not adequately carried out its responsibilities on this river. We would be able to obtain full utilization of all the resources that this river can afford. We would see a little harbour development in Burnaby, along the Pitt river and along the eastern end of the Fraser river. Up to now this river has been developed in a slipshod and haphazard manner; there has been no element of design attached to it. However, it is now time that we should realize we are either going to continue the mess we are in now or we are going to begin to utilize the river in such a manner as the ingenuity of the people concerned can best accomplish.
I should like to pass on two other thoughts. I hope the minister will at some time consider asking that the corporation of Burnaby, which has a railroad running through the centre of it, be supplied with a railway station if for no other purpose than to load and unload passengers and take on express. After all, the city of Toronto has all kinds of places where the trains stop on the way to and from the city. Montreal has the same facilities. We are asking for the same thing in Burnaby. We do not like to go through heavy traffic for many miles to the railway stations at New Westminster or Vancouver.
I should like to thank the department for deciding against locating an auxiliary airport in my riding. The people in my riding have long been apprehensive lest the quiet of their homes be disturbed by the noise and by the danger which is involved in living next door to an airfield. I understand that the department has now developed an auxiliary airport in the Pitt Meadows area and I should like the minister if possible to give a report on the progress being made in the development of that airfield.

Mr. Chairman, I know the committee is anxious to pass this main item. I will therefore move directly to the local matter I wish to raise.
In the constituency of Northumberland-Miramichi there has been a continuing problem facing the department in connection with the dominion government telephone line which
[Mr. Regier.l
serves the area from Black river bridge to Escuminac on the south side of Miramichi bay.
There is a heavy concentration in this area of people who are engaged for the most part in the fishing industry and who reside, in the main, along the Chatham-Escuminac highway. Their only means of telecommunication is the federal government telephone line. This telephone line was constructed many years ago, primarily as an aid to navigation as a connection link between Chatham and the marine lighthouse at Escuminac point but also for the dispatch of pilots from shore to ship to guide ocean going steamers to inshore ports along the Miramichi river for cargoes of lumber, and to relay notification of the steamer's arrival at point Escuminac to transport and customs and excise officials at Chatham.
This telephone line has never been properly equipped to a point that assured services under all conditions, despite the concentrated efforts of the maintenance crew and the diligent work of the board operators. Over the years the department has expended moneys for the upkeep of the line but expenditures were never sufficient to bring it to the standard of other telephone systems operating in the province.
The department's expenditures may have been based on the revenue derived from this line. I know that revenues have decreased of late years and that collections have been difficult. One reason why collections have been poor and why patrons whose accounts were always promptly paid have discontinued the service is the poor service rendered, particularly at nights.
In the first place the equipment is not adequate to provide uninterrupted service. Many times there has been no service for periods of two and three days and on occasions for a full week. Another reason-and a very important one- is that the service is operated only during day time. During the night it is not possible to contact a clergyman or doctor or nurse. When medical care is required during the night there is no way to contact the closest doctor at Chatham, up to 30 miles away, except by driving over the highway and during storms in the wintertime that is almost impossible.
For several years I have made representations to the department outlining existing conditions and urging that the line be adequately equipped. The situation is becoming worse even to the point of a curtailment in the hours during which operators are on duty. The department should either provide adequate service or offer their franchise and equipment to a public utility company, as a solution which I previously advanced to the

department. Even if the department turned over the entire equipment gratis and granted a subsidy in respect of the telephone service for the lighthouse and pilots, the government would save money.
Telephone service in this area is away out of step with the standard enjoyed in other places. It is an important fishing area and adequate telephone connections are essential for this and other obvious reasons. Even the British empire lightweight champion, Yvon Durelle, who lives in this area has to drive to Chatham to make his telephone contacts. It is difficult to realize that in the year 1958 a well-populated area settled hundreds of years ago is so inadequately served. I trust the minister will see to it that this area receives telephone service in keeping with modern day requirements and that this problem will not be sidestepped further by small annual expenditures that only put salve on the sore.

Mr. Chairman, on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Transport I should like to inquire of the minister whether or not it is his intention to proceed at this session with the resolution standing on the order paper in his name to amend the Transport Act to provide for the appointment of a transport controller. I ask this in view of the great interest that has been taken in the Bracken royal commission on boxcars and their distribution. As people who are acquainted with this problem well know, if any major step is to be taken to provide a fair basis for the distribution of boxcars at elevator points in the prairie region it is quite possible and indeed almost likely that authority such as is requested in this resolution would be required.
I can see no reason the government might have had for placing this resolution on the order paper other than its belief that this power was needed as a result of the pending report of the Bracken commission. If it is needed or if it is likely to be needed then I feel the legislation should be passed during this session. If on the other hand the government knows that Mr. John Bracken in his report will not be suggesting anything that will require such power or will not be making any recommendation that will require such power before the next session of parliament then I do not feel there is any reason for the government to go forward with this resolution. In other words, if the government believes the power that would flow from having passed this measure is required, I for one am fully prepared to support it. If on the other hand the government believes that this power is not necessary between now and the next session of parliament then 57071-3-274

I can see no reason for proceeding. I should like the minister to tell me whether it is needed in the light of any report that may be made by the Bracken commission.

I am very glad to answer that question, Mr. Chairman. Since introducing this legislation I have looked into the matter very carefully and I can see no indication of any need for such legislation between now and the next session of parliament and so I have withdrawn the legislation.
