I believe the minister has taken a very reasonable position. I am not asking the minister to comment on this but it would suggest to me very definitely that Mr. John Bracken will not be reporting anything to the government that would require this type of power between now and the next session of parliament. I realize, of course, that other powers may be available, for example, under the Canadian Wheat Board Act or that a solution could be found through some measure other than the one to which the minister referred.
I wish to support all those organizations, provincial governments and members of this house who have impressed upon the government the need to provide a toll-free seaway. The people of the prairies and industries in eastern Canada have looked forward to the establishment of the St. Lawrence seaway as a means of providing great savings to their industries and have shared the hope that on the completion of the seaway it would be made toll-free. They are disturbed not only by the report of the minister that tolls will be levied on the seaway but also by the reported possibility that tolls may be levied on the Welland canal. They believe this is a retrograde step and something the government should resist. Knowing the many statements made by hon. members of the Conservative party in the past to the effect that they would support Canadian interests when they came into conflict with United States interests, I express the hope that the Canadian government will exert its influence to make the seaway toll-free.
I have examined a number of submissions that have been made in this regard by many organizations and I find the body of opinion supporting a toll-free seaway is very substantial indeed. Representations have been made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, by the interprovincial farm union council and by a well known and important newspaper of this country, the Globe and Mail, which, in spite of a few screwball editorials and a recent one in particular which comes to my mind, is in my opinion a newspaper of very

Supply-Transport
high stature in Canada. I believe it is becoming, as it were, Canada's New York Times. In a thoughtful editorial in the Globe and Mail in the issue of July 29 it is pointed out that there should be no tolls on the Welland canal.
Also in opposition to tolls on the Welland canal are the great lakes fleet owners, the Steel Company of Canada, the Niagara Peninsula communities, the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Manitoba. Indeed, a very large percentage of the Canadian public as represented by these organizations and provincial governments believe that Canada's policy should be a toll-free seaway.
The Minister of Transport in the past has given his version of what a system of tolls might save in the way of lower freight rates on grain. The people of the prairies are naturally interested in the St. Lawrence seaway in the hope that it will reduce their freight rate burden both on goods being shipped to the west and on goods being shipped to the east and particularly on grain shipments. They have noted with a great deal of concern as I am sure the government also has that the route through Port Arthur and Fort William, through the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river, in relation to the west route through Vancouver, in recent years has become relatively uneconomical for the movement of grain.
When appearing before the agriculture committee of this house during this session the chairman of the Canadian wheat board W. C. MacNamara gave figures relating to the cost of shipping through various routes. We were informed that to ship wheat from Fort William to Montreal cost 22\ cents a bushel. To trans-ship this wheat to the United Kingdom from Montreal costs 14.4 cents a bushel. On the other hand, the total rate out of Vancouver to the United Kingdom is only 18 cents a bushel that is compared with the total eastern rate of more than 36 cents a bushel.
The minister said that the St. Lawrence seaway would result in a saving of 4 cents a bushel to the shippers of wheat. In the agricultural committee I asked the chairman of the wheat board the following question:
Do you know whether or not the saving might be in the neighbourhood of 4 or 5 cents a bushel?
To this question the chairman of the Canadian wheat board replied:
No. I think that is anybody's guess. I will be pleasantly surprised if it results in a saving of 4 cents per bushel for our producers.
I should like the minister, if he can, to give the committee the assurance once again that the use of the St. Lawrence seaway will result in a minimum saving of 4 cents a bushel. I know that the minister must have

had very good grounds for making this statement but I also believe that the chairman of the Canadian wheat board is an expert on all matters relating to wheat and it was disturbing to me to hear him state that he would be pleasantly surprised if the seaway results in a saving of 4 cents per bushel. I repeat my suggestion to the minister that in so far as possible the St. Lawrence seaway should be toll free.
There is another matter I wish to raise on item one of these estimates. I refer to the whole question of C.N.R. lay-offs and the policy of the C.N.R. with regard thereto. On previous occasions I have raised during this session the matter of lay-offs by the C.N.R. at various shops across the country and in reply to my questions the Minister of Transport has always said that he would be quite prepared to discuss the matter with the C.N.R. management. While I have no doubt that the minister has always discussed this matter with the C.N.R. following requests in the house, little seems to have been gained by these discussions and the lay-offs are continuing.
The lay-offs seem to be taking place at a large number of points across Canada. I have in my hand a letter from the Moncton and district labour council sent to me on June 13 of this year which reads in part as follows:
Commencing a short time after the election, layoffs in the C.N.R. have been constant-small, but constant. There is every indication that the eventual padlocking of the C.N.R. shops in Moncton is on the planning board.
That is a very strong statement made by J. E. McAllister, secretary of the Moncton and district labour council. He goes on to say, and I believe this has been discussed before in the house, that the Minister of Transport, according to newspaper reports and in statements made during television appearances, had assured the people of Moncton that this thing would not happen in the future. I think it is time that the C.N.R. and the minister gave the people who are employed by the railway company some indication whether or not they can look forward to a reasonable degree of security in their work in the months and years that lie ahead.
I know it will be said that nothing can stop progress and nothing should stop progress, and that these people are merely casualties because of technological improvement. That may be an answer that satisfies some people but it does not satisfy the men who are affected. If Canada had a full employment economy at the present time these men could look for comparable opportunities in other industries and the complaint would not be

nearly so serious. But there is every danger, in spite of anything that has been said, that as these men are laid off they will be added to the unemployed rolls in the country. Perhaps I might make reference to an article that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of Saturday, July 15, 1958. The writer is Michael Harris and he is dealing with a statement made by Mr. George D. Battigelli, secretary-treasurer of district lodge No. 2, international association of machinists, railroad division. The article reads in part as follows:
As eh example of progressive reductions, he cited the proposed lay-offs at the Stratford, Ont. shops- 150 men at July 11, 70 at August 1, 70 at September 1, 60 at October 1, and 200 between April 1 and October 1, 1959-making a total of 550 shop craftsmen. These cuts will involve machinists, electricians, pipefitters, painters, carpenters, sheet metal workers, blacksmiths' helpers and other helpers and apprentices. Mr. Battigelli thinks the Stratford shops will be closed down before those at Fort Rouge.
Earlier in the article it is pointed out that C.N.R. employees at Winnipeg are very concerned about the rising lay-offs at the C.N.R. shops, particularly the Fort Rouge shop, and the report that this shop will be entirely closed in the future. I have merely given these examples of C.N.R. lay-offs to impress upon the minister again the importance of giving the House of Commons and these employees something more tangible by way of an answer than the answer we have heard heretofore, namely that the minister will discuss the matter with the C.N.R. management, without any indication being given that anything was done as a result of his representations.
If these changes are necessary in the future it would seem to me that as long as we have widespread unemployment the lay-offs should be postponed until employment picks up. From the national standpoint I can see no advantage in putting these people on the unemployed rolls now merely to draw unemployment insurance or to be a burden on the country in some other way. It would seem to me that it would be logical at this time for the government to do everything possible to see that these people retain their jobs. When the minister replies I hope he will be able to give the men who have been or may be affected greater encouragement than he has been able to give in the past.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question before he resumes his seat?
Yes.

I do not think that at all. I for one do not feel that you can play the interests of one part of Canada against the interests of another. I am in favour of steps being taken that will improve the economic standards of people in all parts of Canada. One of the main reasons there is widespread unemployment across the nation today is the fact that the prairie grain producers are in a state of recession. I know that members of the government, including the Minister of Transport, have given very careful consideration recently to some help for the grain producers.
But I would suggest with great respect to the government that they should do a whole lot better in this regard than has been indicated by certain leaks in the newspapers to date. If they did that, it would take care of some of the problems to which my hon. friend has referred.

I should like to answer the two questions which the hon. member for Assini-boia put to me. First, he was asking me to guarantee a saving of four cents a bushel on grain being moved from the lakehead to Montreal. This, of course, I cannot do and never intended to do. When I was asked I said the best estimate I was able to make, based on the best economic information I was able to obtain, was that it was hoped and expected that the saving on a bushel of grain being transferred from the lakehead to Montreal would be four cents. Naturally, I cannot guarantee anything of that kind. All I can do is to give the best estimate available to me to make.
Secondly, the hon. member asked me to give some assurance to the workers on the Canadian National that their jobs would remain intact. This, of course, is another thing, as I think the hon. member knows, but it is impossible for me to do. The management of the railway is, by statute, responsible for all matters to do with the running of the railway. I have, as I have told my hon. friend and other members in this house when questions about Canadian National employment have been brought up, in every case brought these cases to the attention of the management and have discussed them with the management. The management has assured me, as I have informed the house, that wherever it is possible to keep an employee working, that is done. Employees are only let out very reluctantly and when there is absolutely no work for an employee to do. I am afraid I cannot give the hon. member or the house any more

Supply-Transport
information about future employment possibilities on the Canadian National than that.

I think that if it is impossible for the minister, through his negotiations, to give us any more assurance than he has been able to do tonight, then surely it is the responsibility of the government to provide in Canada an economy in which there is full employment. We have gone over the cabinet ministers, almost one by one, during this session to try to find out if one of the cabinet ministers or the government itself had any plan or any program to provide full employment in this country. I, for one, have heard nothing of any program that would suggest to me that full employment was something to which we could look forward in the near future. As a matter of fact, there has been no indication yet that the government has a winter employment program, and without an adequate winter program the fears of the people who may face lay-offs from the Canadian National shops are, of course, greatly increased.
I wonder if I may ask the minister a question as to whether, as a result of his discussions with Canadian National management, he can assure the house and the workers involved in Winnipeg that the report by Mr. A. J. Crofts and the Winnipeg Free Press of July 15 to the effect that, the Fort Rouge shops at Winnipeg will be closed by 1960, is not correct? Apparently the newspaper has some information as to the planning and program of the Canadian National. I would think the minister would be able to get, without difficulty, information from the Canadian National about its plans for the shops in Winnipeg, the Strathcona and Fort Rouge shops. Apparently the chief concern at this time is that further lay-offs will be made and that by 1960 there will be a complete closing of the Fort Rouge shops.

In answer to that question, I may say that I am aware of no such plan. I shall be glad to speak to the management of the Canadian National to ascertain if any such plan exists, but I have not heard of it.
I wonder if the minister, either in the house or by letter, would communicate to me the result of his discussion with the management?
Yes, I shall be glad to do that, Mr. Chairman.

I just want to take a few moments of the committee's time to bring to the attention of the minister one or two points concerning my own riding. I should like, first of all, to talk about the city of Corner Brook and the facilities which are needed

there. Corner Brook is the second city in Newfoundland. It is the site of, if not the largest the second largest integrated newsprint mill in the world. In addition to that, it is also a transshipping point for the northern coast of western Newfoundland. For these two reasons, there is within that area a great deal of shipping, by rail and by boat.
I know that at the moment improvements are being made to the railyard, improvements which I believe will add much to the facilities of the area. However, there is one fear that the people within the city have, and that is that it is possible to have this yard expanded, then have some type of dock built there, and to arrive at a position where there is a good dock and a railyard and yet the one is not complementary to the other because of the locations. I wonder if, when we come to the proper item of the minister's estimates, he would be able to give some information regarding the Canadian National railyard at Corner Brook.
The Canadian National now maintains the old public building which exists in the city of Corner Brook. I believe they rent part of it to the provincial government. I should like to suggest to the minister that he, in turn, suggest to the Canadian National that one improvement that could be made in the Canadian National service within the city is to have a ticket office installed in that old public building. Actually the railway station is a little out of the way. It is down on the waterfront, which is a very busy section. I think it would be extremely convenient to the travelling public if they were able to go to an office in the public building, which is in the central part of the city, and there buy railway tickets or make reservations which they want to make. I seriously make that recommendation to the minister in the hope he will, in turn, make it to the officials of the Canadian National.
Undoubtedly, the minister is aware, and I am sure the officials of his department are, that at various times within the port of Corner Brook we have a serious icebreaking problem. Following the winter of 1956-51 it was well into the month of June before ships were able to move newsprint from the port of Corner Brook to the markets of the world. Various representations have beer made by the company, by the unions anc by other bodies, both to the minister and tc the officials of his department for icebreaking service in that area. In the spring of 1957 th< mill was completely tied up because it wa: impossible to ship by boat. We were fortunah at that time in being able to secure th< services of a United States navy icebreaker the U.S.S. Edisto, which was able to comi into Corner Brook and break the ice there

Afterwards, we were able to look after it ourselves. In the meantime we also had the service of the icebreaker N.B. McLean, which did a fine job around that section of the coast in breaking the ice and starting off spring transportation. May I digress here for a moment to pay tribute to the captains and crews of both the U.S.S. Edisto and the N.B. McLean for the fine job that was done at that particular time.
May I once again urge the minister that in making his plans for icebreaking both in the lower St. Lawrence and on the west coast of Newfoundland particular attention be given to a problem which can be a serious one if the port is blocked by ice during the winter period. If the port is blocked for any prolonged period the company is not able to ship its paper. Neither are the various commercial concerns able to bring in commodities as cheaply as they can by water. The result is that in the paper industry, where the market is very competitive at the moment, 12 per cent is added to the cost of the paper. Considering the many other transportation costs in Newfoundland this added expense results in a cost which is very restrictive in the paper industry of Newfoundland. I would therefore urge the minister to give consideration to this problem of icebreaking within bay of Islands and the port of Corner Brook.
Before I leave the C.N.R. there is one other thing I should like to say. Dotted along the railway line in Newfoundland are small flag stations. These stations are not looked after by a caretaker. The station is just a small building where people can wait to board a train or where a small quantity of freight can be taken off a train or where freight can be put to be loaded on the train upon its arrival. These small flag stations dotted across the country are sometimes found to be in a state of serious disrepair. It would cost very little to have these small buildings kept in good repair all the year round. I should like to suggest to the minister than an effort be made to have these small flag stations repaired and painted. That procedure would add to the appearance of the C.N.R. property along the line.
We have down the northern coast of Newfoundland an area which, over the past few years, has had very little telegraph and telephone communication. The service there now is not only incompatible with present day needs but it does not even measure up to the standard which was experienced by people 30 years ago. Many representations have been made to the Canadian National Telegraphs and every time the reply is given that the cost of installing the necessary equipment is so great, compared with the revenue which
Supply-Transport
could be derived, that they feel they are not prepared to make the necessary outlay.
I would suggest to the minister that somewhere between the aims of a commercial body trying to make a profit and a government body trying to operate a service for the people there arises the question of service. I would hope that the minister would either get the Canadian National Telegraphs to look into this problem or the Department of Transport itself to take over this area and service the telegraph and telephone services as it is doing in some other places. The area to which I refer is the area on the west coast of Newfoundland north of Bonne bay on the Port au Port peninsula and the area from St. George's west to the Codray valley. These areas are very poorly served by telegraph and by telephone. If there is no other solution, if the Canadian National Telegraphs is not able to handle the problem I would hope that some arrangement can be made with the Department of Transport to have this matter looked into and promptly dealt with.
Last year the Department of Transport was able to build on Kepple island near Port Saunders on the St. Barbe coast a very fine lighthouse and fog horn and a residence for the keeper. To date however this installation is not working. I should like to recommend to the minister that this installation be put into operation at the earliest possible date. It is an important one. Many of the ships that travel up and down the coast such as the C.N.R. boats have their navigation aids such as radar and so on. However the smaller boats have no navigational aids and they need the services which this lighthouse and the fog alarm are able to give.
During the debate on this first item of the estimates of the Department of Transport we have heard on more than one occasion today mention of the motor vessel William Carson. I understand that the William Carson went into Port aux Basques yesterday. I would hope that when we come to that particular item the minister will be able to give us some report on that trial run. Although it has not been stated it has been intimated that possibly it will be found that the harbour at Port aux Basques is not suitable for the William Carson and that maybe some other port will have to be found.
Let me first say-and here I agree with my colleague the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo-that in the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada it was agreed that this ferry should operate from North Sydney to Port aux Basques. If, however, it should happen that the harbour at Port aux Basques is not found to be suitable for the William Carson, it is my belief that the only alternative port for the William Carson would be

Supply-Transport
that of Corner Brook. Here there are rail facilities. For those who are travelling by boat there are hotel facilities. It would be an admirable solution to a difficult problem should the port of Port aux Basques be found unsuitable for the motor vessel William Carson.
I have a number of other small questions, Mr. Chairman, but I think I shall leave those until we come to the particular items.

Because of the rapidly increasing traffic in small craft from the Grand Coulee dam on the Columbia in the United States to as far north as Revelstoke I would urge that every consideration be given to installing aids to navigation. There has been some improvement in recent years, but the minister probably knows the channel between the international boundary and Castle-gar. In that channel there is a nine knot current with rocks at various places in the river and one has to follow a careful course in order to keep out of difficulty. There is also a need for good markers between

Cottonwood point in the Narrows and West Demars also between Arrowhead and Revelstoke. I mention this on behalf of a number of local organizations and also on behalf of an increasing number of United States tourists who are using small craft and, in some cases, quite large cruisers on these waters.
About four years ago at the request of one of the captains on the steamer I took a trip down the whole river. I know the river like a book. He was interested to find out how many buoys and reflectors were missing. I found 11 buoys out of place in one very bad channel, and a number of shore reflectors were gone. The person who had been paid to do the work had apparently not been on the job for a year; he had not been near the buoys or the reflectors. That situation has now been corrected but I suggest that a thorough survey be made of the river in view of the increasing traffic and satisfactory aids to navigation should be put in which would be understood by persons operating small craft. I was wondering whether any chart is provided for the guidance of persons operating small craft coming from the United States containing information as to the meaning of the buoys-black, red or striped-or as to the meaning of certain reflectors, because a 100-foot deviation from the true channel could mean the wrecking of any one of these small vessels.
I will have to consult the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys who are in charge of the hydrographic survey to find out if such charts are available.

In view of this very interesting and rapidly increasing traffic, if no chart is available could the minister see that some simple chart is provided for people coming up the river so they would know what the different markings mean?
I will ask about that.

426. Steamship inspection service, including the carrying out of the provisions of the conventions for the safety of life at sea and load lines and contributions as detailed in the estimates, $999,901.

I am sorry to interrupt again, but I have been asked to bring this question to the attention of the minister. I want to speak on lifesaving equipment very briefly and ask a question or two. We all know that because of the great increase in the number of small craft on all the rivers and lakes of Canada there has been a necessity for legislation providing for regulations and licensing. This has created a very improved situation, and I want to compliment the minister and his officials on "Safety Afloat". I have distributed a goodly number around the

constituency to launch clubs and boat owners and people of that sort and they appreciated it very much.
However, I do want to say this: The present life jackets that are approved by the Department of Transport are not altogether satisfactory. They are satisfactory on large vessels where you have time to put them on and adjust and tie them but they are not satisfactory for use on small craft. In the first place they are most uncomfortable to wear all the time. Secondly, accidents in small craft occur very quickly and there is little or no time to tie the blasted things on. In addition to that I want to point out I have been informed by some ladies that they are most uncomfortable to wear in the boat and most difficult to adjust at times-to put it as delicately as possible-owing to the contours of their bodies. I have some experience in that field-I mean boating. I mention that seriously.
There is a type of jacket or vest without sleeves that can be worn with comfort. I make a point of having the family put these on. Not only are they comfortable but, as far as I know, they are practical and safe but I understand these vests or jackets are not approved or recommended by the department at the present time. I suggest that there should be some further study made of the value of these jackets and with regard to their being recommended to the public at large as well as with respect to their improvement.
In recent months in Canada there have been a number of cases where persons were found drowned on account of accidents in small boats and who were discovered in the water wearing the standard type of life jacket but put on improperly; their heads were in the water, and so on. It is a serious matter and I believe the department should give further consideration to it and educate the public to understand that these vests or jackets are approved by the department and are the best thing to wear. The department should urge people to wear them when boating. If this were done I believe we would reduce the number of deaths through boating accidents.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer the hon. member on that question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shouldn't!

I believe the answer is that if people are going out in small craft in dangerous weather that is rough or windy they should put on their life jackets before they go out. Secondly, we try to bring this to the attention of the public in our booklet entitled, "Safety Afloat". Thirdly, we have a committee of the department which is working constantly with the boating industry and the 57071-3-275
Supply-Transport
